questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: An unmodified (clean) audit opinion on financial statements communicates that

answers.text: The financial statements are presented fairly, in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework
The auditor has verified that every transaction in the financial statements is correct
The financial statements contain no misstatements of any kind, including immaterial ones
The entity's internal controls over financial reporting are effective

explanations.a: AU-C Section 700 specifies that an unmodified opinion states that the financial statements 'present fairly, in all material respects' the financial position, results of operations, and cash flows in accordance with the applicable framework. The 'in all material respects' qualifier acknowledges that the audit provides reasonable — not absolute — assurance, and that immaterial misstatements may exist without affecting the opinion.
explanations.b: An audit does not verify every transaction — it uses sampling and risk-based procedures to reach a conclusion about the financial statements as a whole. An unmodified opinion does not represent transaction-by-transaction verification.
explanations.c: An unmodified opinion does not guarantee that the financial statements are free of all misstatements. The opinion is expressed in terms of material misstatement — immaterial errors may exist and are not reflected in the opinion.
explanations.d: For a standard financial statement audit of a nonissuer, the audit opinion addresses the financial statements — not internal controls. An opinion on the effectiveness of ICFR is expressed separately in an integrated audit under PCAOB standards.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A qualified audit opinion is appropriate when

answers.text: The auditor disagrees with management on every significant accounting estimate
The entity has changed its accounting principle from one period to the next, requiring an emphasis-of-matter paragraph
The auditor has identified material weaknesses in internal control over financial reporting

Either (1) the financial statements contain a material misstatement that is not pervasive, or (2) the auditor was unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and the possible effect is material but not pervasive

explanations.a: Disagreement with every significant accounting estimate would indicate pervasive misstatement — which would more likely lead to an adverse opinion rather than a qualified opinion. A qualified opinion applies to material-but-not-pervasive issues.
explanations.b: An accounting principle change that is properly disclosed with appropriate retrospective adjustment is addressed by an emphasis-of-matter paragraph in an unmodified report — not a qualified opinion. Consistency changes handled in conformity with GAAP do not require opinion modification.
explanations.c: Material weaknesses in internal control are communicated to management and TCWG through a written communication under AU-C 265 — they do not automatically result in a qualified opinion on the financial statements. A material weakness affects the integrated audit ICFR opinion for issuers but does not itself cause a modification of the financial statement opinion.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 705 specifies two circumstances for a qualified opinion: (1) the auditor concludes that misstatements are material but not pervasive — the 'except for' opinion addresses the specific departure while affirming the fairness of the rest of the financial statements; and (2) the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and the possible effect of undetected misstatements could be material but not pervasive — a scope-limitation qualified opinion.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: An adverse audit opinion is issued when

answers.text: The auditor concludes that misstatements are both material AND pervasive — the financial statements as a whole do not present fairly in accordance with the applicable framework
Management refuses to sign the written representations letter
The auditor identifies one material misstatement in a single account balance
The auditor detects evidence of intentional fraud by management

explanations.a: AU-C Section 705 requires an adverse opinion when the auditor concludes that misstatements are both material and pervasive to the financial statements taken as a whole. The adverse opinion states that the financial statements 'do not present fairly' — the strongest possible negative conclusion, reserved for situations where the departure from the framework is so fundamental that the financial statements are misleading as a whole.
explanations.b: Management's refusal to sign the representations letter creates a scope limitation (and may raise questions about management integrity) — but it results in a qualified opinion or disclaimer, not an adverse opinion. An adverse opinion requires that the auditor has concluded the financial statements are materially misstated, not merely that a procedural requirement was unmet.
explanations.c: A single material misstatement in one account balance — if it does not affect the financial statements as a whole in a pervasive manner — would result in a qualified opinion ('except for' this specific item), not an adverse opinion. Pervasiveness means the misstatement affects many elements of the financial statements or relates to disclosures fundamental to user understanding.
explanations.d: Evidence of intentional fraud does not automatically result in an adverse opinion. The auditor must evaluate whether the fraud resulted in material and pervasive misstatements. Depending on the nature and magnitude of the fraud's financial effect, the resulting opinion could be qualified, adverse, or (if sufficient evidence cannot be obtained) a disclaimer.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: reporting on audit engagements (emphasis-of-matter and other-matter paragraphs)
questions.text: An auditor includes an emphasis-of-matter (EOM) paragraph in the audit report. What is the primary purpose of this paragraph, and does it modify the audit opinion?

answers.text: An EOM paragraph modifies the audit opinion — it signals that the financial statements contain a material departure from the applicable framework
An EOM paragraph is used to describe the scope of the audit and replaces the standard scope paragraph in the audit report
An EOM paragraph is used when the financial statements are not in accordance with GAAP — it describes the specific departure without issuing a qualified opinion

An EOM paragraph draws users' attention to a matter already presented or disclosed in the financial statements that is fundamental to user understanding — it does NOT modify the audit opinion, which remains unmodified

explanations.a: An EOM paragraph does not modify the audit opinion — it accompanies an unmodified opinion. Opinion modification (qualified, adverse, disclaimer) occurs when misstatements exist or evidence is insufficient. An EOM paragraph highlights information already properly presented in the financial statements without questioning the overall fairness of the financial statements.
explanations.b: An EOM paragraph is not a replacement for the scope paragraph — the scope paragraph describes audit procedures while an EOM paragraph highlights specific information from the financial statements. Both may appear in the same report.
explanations.c: When financial statements contain departures from GAAP, the appropriate response is opinion modification (qualified or adverse) — not an EOM paragraph. EOM paragraphs are used alongside unmodified opinions to highlight properly disclosed information, not to describe improper accounting.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 706 defines emphasis-of-matter paragraphs as additional communications the auditor includes to draw users' attention to information already presented or disclosed in the financial statements that is, in the auditor's judgment, of such importance that it is fundamental to users' understanding. Examples include: going concern explanations (referring to management's disclosures about the going concern uncertainty), significant events disclosed in the notes, or accounting changes. The EOM paragraph does not modify the opinion — the financial statements are still fairly presented; the EOM simply highlights a specific important matter.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: reporting on audit engagements (emphasis-of-matter and other-matter paragraphs)
questions.text: An auditor includes an other-matter (OM) paragraph in an audit report. How does an other-matter paragraph differ from an emphasis-of-matter paragraph?

answers.text: An OM paragraph modifies the opinion while an EOM paragraph does not modify the opinion

An OM paragraph draws attention to matters relevant to users' understanding that are NOT presented or disclosed in the financial statements themselves — while an EOM paragraph highlights matters already presented in the financial statements
An OM paragraph is required when financial statements include comparative periods while an EOM paragraph is optional in all circumstances
An OM paragraph and an EOM paragraph are interchangeable terms for the same type of communication in modern GAAS

explanations.a: Neither an EOM nor an OM paragraph modifies the audit opinion. Both are informational additions to the report that do not affect the opinion's form (unmodified, qualified, adverse, or disclaimer). If opinion modification is required, the appropriate modified opinion paragraph is used instead.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 706 distinguishes the two types: (1) Emphasis-of-matter paragraph — refers to information already presented or disclosed in the financial statements that the auditor believes is fundamental to user understanding (e.g., a note about substantial doubt regarding going concern); (2) Other-matter paragraph — refers to matters that are not presented or disclosed in the financial statements but are relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities, or the audit report. Examples of OM use include: explaining that the prior-period financial statements were audited by a predecessor auditor; communicating that the report is restricted to specified parties; or noting that certain information required by the regulatory body is presented as supplementary information only.
explanations.c: Comparative period financial statements do not automatically require an OM paragraph. The situation of a predecessor auditor is one specific OM scenario for comparative statements — but many comparative statement situations have no additional paragraphs at all. The distinction is about the source of the information (in vs. not in the financial statements), not about comparative periods.
explanations.d: EOM and OM are distinct paragraph types with different purposes and different triggers. GAAS (AU-C 706) defines them separately and applies them to different circumstances.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: reporting on audit engagements (emphasis-of-matter and other-matter paragraphs)
questions.text: An auditor's report on Ridgeline Corp's financial statements includes two additional paragraphs: (1) a paragraph highlighting the company's substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern, which is also discussed in Note 8; and (2) a paragraph disclosing that the prior-year comparative financial statements were audited by a different firm that issued an unmodified opinion. How should each of these paragraphs be classified?

answers.text: Paragraph 1 is an emphasis-of-matter paragraph — the going concern matter is disclosed in Note 8, already in the financial statements; Paragraph 2 is an other-matter paragraph — the predecessor auditor's work is not presented or disclosed in the financial statements themselves
Both paragraphs are emphasis-of-matter paragraphs since both relate to matters that affect users' understanding of the financial statements
Both paragraphs are other-matter paragraphs since both introduce additional information beyond the basic financial statements
Paragraph 1 is an other-matter paragraph since it relates to going concern; Paragraph 2 is an emphasis-of-matter paragraph since it relates to prior-year auditors

explanations.a: This correctly applies the AU-C 706 distinction: (1) The going concern paragraph draws attention to information that already appears in Note 8 of the financial statements — it is an emphasis-of-matter paragraph, used to highlight matter presented in the financial statements; (2) The predecessor auditor paragraph introduces information about the prior-year audit that does not appear in the financial statements (the financial statements themselves contain comparative numbers but do not disclose who audited the prior year) — it is an other-matter paragraph, introducing information not in the financial statements. The key test: Is the information already in the financial statements (EOM) or not (OM)?
explanations.b: Not both paragraphs are EOM. The predecessor auditor paragraph introduces information about who performed the prior-year audit — this does not appear in the financial statements themselves and is therefore an other-matter paragraph, not an emphasis-of-matter paragraph.
explanations.c: Not both paragraphs are OM. The going concern paragraph refers specifically to Note 8, which is part of the financial statements. When the auditor is directing attention to existing financial statement content, the paragraph is an emphasis-of-matter paragraph.
explanations.d: This reverses the correct classification. Going concern information that appears in the notes is highlighted by an EOM paragraph (information IS in the financial statements). Predecessor auditor information that is not in the financial statements is communicated through an OM paragraph.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: An attestation examination engagement under SSAE 18 (AT-C Section 205) differs from a financial statement audit primarily because

answers.text: Attestation examinations provide less assurance than financial statement audits
Attestation examinations are performed only by non-CPA practitioners

Attestation examinations involve subject matter other than financial statements — such as internal controls, sustainability reports, or compliance with specified criteria — governed by SSAE 18, while financial statement audits are governed by GAAS (Statements on Auditing Standards)
Attestation examinations are restricted-use reports that can only be provided to the engaging party, never to third parties

explanations.a: Both attestation examinations and financial statement audits provide reasonable assurance — the highest attainable level of assurance in their respective frameworks. An attestation examination does not provide less assurance than an audit; the distinction is the type of subject matter and the governing standards, not the level of assurance.
explanations.b: Attestation engagements under SSAE 18 are performed by CPAs. The CPA's expertise, independence, and professional standards govern attestation engagements — non-CPA practitioners do not perform SSAE 18 engagements.
explanations.c: The key distinction is the subject matter and the governing standards: (1) Financial statement audits address whether historical financial statements are fairly presented — governed by GAAS (SASs issued by the AICPA Auditing Standards Board) or PCAOB standards for issuers; (2) Attestation examination engagements address whether specified subject matter — which may be internal controls (SOC 2), environmental disclosures, compliance assertions, or other non-financial-statement subject matter — conforms to identified criteria. Attestation engagements are governed by SSAE 18 (AT-C Sections 205, 210, 215).
explanations.d: Attestation examination reports under AT-C 205 are not inherently restricted-use. Reports on subject matter based on criteria available to all users (general use criteria) may be general-use reports. Restriction applies to agreed-upon procedures (AT-C 215) and to engagements using criteria not generally available — not to all attestation examinations.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: An attestation review engagement under SSAE 18 (AT-C Section 210) provides which level of assurance, and how is the conclusion expressed?

answers.text: Reasonable assurance — the practitioner expresses a positive-form opinion
Absolute assurance — the practitioner certifies the subject matter is accurate
No assurance — the practitioner reports findings only, leaving users to draw their own conclusions
Limited assurance — the practitioner expresses a conclusion in negative form, stating that nothing came to their attention indicating the subject matter is not in accordance with the criteria

explanations.a: Reasonable assurance and a positive-form opinion describe an attestation examination (AT-C 205) — not an attestation review. The review provides a lower level of assurance than an examination.
explanations.b: Absolute assurance is unattainable in any professional engagement. No attestation standard provides for certification of accuracy with absolute certainty.
explanations.c: No assurance and findings-only describes an agreed-upon procedures engagement (AT-C 215) — not an attestation review. The review provides limited assurance expressed through a conclusion.
explanations.d: AT-C Section 210 specifies that an attestation review provides limited assurance — a level of assurance that is lower than that obtained in an examination but higher than no assurance. The conclusion is expressed in negative form: the practitioner states that based on the review, nothing came to their attention that caused them to believe the subject matter is not in accordance with the identified criteria. This 'negative assurance' approach parallels the SSARS review conclusion for financial statements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: For an attestation engagement to be valid under SSAE 18, which three elements must be present?

answers.text: A written engagement letter, a management representation letter, and an engagement team with at least one partner-level practitioner

A responsible party with appropriate capability, suitable and available criteria, and measurable subject matter — together enabling the practitioner to evaluate the subject matter against the criteria and express a conclusion
A publicly registered client, an independent board of directors, and a formal internal audit department
A prior-year attestation report, comparative subject matter, and a specialist's opinion on the technical aspects of the subject matter

explanations.a: A written engagement letter and management representations are procedural requirements for attestation engagements, but they are not the three fundamental elements that define whether an attestation engagement can be performed. The three elements relate to the structure of the engagement itself — the parties, the subject matter, and the criteria.
explanations.b: AT-C Section 105 (the overarching attestation standard) requires three elements for an attestation engagement: (1) Responsible party — a party that is responsible for the subject matter or the assertion about it, and is willing to accept that responsibility (typically management); (2) Suitable and available criteria — a set of benchmarks used to evaluate the subject matter that are objective, measurable, complete, and either established by a recognized body or agreed upon for restricted-use engagements; and (3) Measurable subject matter — the information or condition that the practitioner evaluates against the criteria, which must be capable of consistent measurement. Without all three elements, an attestation engagement cannot be performed.
explanations.c: Publicly registered client status, an independent board, and an internal audit department are entity governance characteristics — they do not define the elements of an attestation engagement. Many attestation engagements are performed for private entities without formal internal audit functions.
explanations.d: A prior-year attestation report, comparative subject matter, and specialist opinion are engagement considerations that may be relevant in certain circumstances — but they are not the three fundamental elements required for an attestation engagement under AT-C 105.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A service organization engages a CPA to examine and report on the design and operating effectiveness of its security and availability controls over a specified period for the benefit of user entities and their auditors. This engagement is BEST described as

answers.text: A SOC 2 Type 2 examination engagement under AT-C Section 205 and the AICPA's criteria for trust services, providing reasonable assurance about the operating effectiveness of controls over the specified period
A financial statement audit under GAAS, expanded to include security and availability controls
An agreed-upon procedures engagement under AT-C Section 215 since the procedures for testing security controls must be specified in advance
A management consulting engagement with no assurance component since security controls are operational rather than financial

explanations.a: This engagement matches the definition of a SOC 2 Type 2 examination: (1) subject matter = a service organization's controls relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, or privacy over a specified period; (2) criteria = AICPA Trust Services Criteria; (3) assurance level = reasonable assurance (examination); (4) period coverage = Type 2 covers both design and operating effectiveness over a period (distinguishing it from Type 1, which covers design at a point in time). The engagement is governed by AT-C Section 205 (Examination Engagements) along with AT-C Section 320 (Reporting on an Examination of Controls at a Service Organization Relevant to User Entities' Internal Control Over Financial Reporting) and the AICPA's Trust Services framework.
explanations.b: GAAS governs financial statement audits — not attestation examinations of service organization security controls. Expanding a financial statement audit to include security controls would not be appropriate — the two engagements have different subject matter, criteria, and standards.
explanations.c: An agreed-upon procedures engagement does not express an opinion or conclusion on the operating effectiveness of controls — the AUP practitioner only reports findings. A SOC 2 report expresses an opinion on control effectiveness, which requires an examination (reasonable assurance) rather than AUP (no assurance).
explanations.d: A SOC 2 examination is an attestation engagement with a formal assurance conclusion — not a management consulting engagement. The practitioner expresses an opinion on whether controls are suitably designed and operating effectively, providing users with meaningful independent assurance.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A company asks a CPA to examine and report on whether its greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions disclosure conforms to a set of criteria developed internally by the company's sustainability team and not published or reviewed by any external body. In evaluating whether this engagement can be accepted, the CPA's PRIMARY concern should be

answers.text: Whether the company's GHG emissions are material to the financial statements — only material information can be the subject of attestation
Whether the company has an internal audit function that has already reviewed the GHG disclosure

Whether the internally developed criteria are suitable and available — criteria developed solely by management for their own disclosure without external validation may lack objectivity, completeness, or verifiability, potentially making the engagement inappropriate
Whether the CPA has prior experience in environmental accounting — specialized experience is required for all non-financial-statement attestation engagements

explanations.a: Materiality to the financial statements is not the threshold for attestation engagements. Attestation addresses subject matter that may include sustainability disclosures, internal controls, and compliance — none of which is limited to financial statement materiality thresholds.
explanations.b: The existence of an internal audit function does not determine whether attestation is possible. Internal audit may have reviewed the GHG disclosure, but the external CPA's attestation provides independent assurance — the criteria question remains fundamental.
explanations.c: AT-C Section 105 requires that suitable criteria be used in attestation engagements. Suitable criteria must be: (1) relevant — pertinent to the subject matter; (2) objective — free from bias; (3) measurable — capable of consistent application; (4) complete — sufficient for evaluating the subject matter; and (5) authoritative — established by a recognized body or sufficiently specific for the purpose. Criteria developed exclusively by management without external review or validation may lack objectivity (management designed them to describe their own practice) and authoritativeness (no external body has endorsed them). The CPA must evaluate whether the criteria meet the suitability requirements before accepting or continuing the engagement.
explanations.d: While relevant expertise enhances audit quality, specialized environmental accounting experience is not a categorical prerequisite for accepting all non-financial attestation engagements. The CPA must have sufficient competence to understand the subject matter and evaluate it against the criteria — which may be achievable through research, training, or use of a specialist. The criteria suitability issue is more fundamental.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: In an agreed-upon procedures (AUP) engagement under AT-C Section 215, the practitioner

answers.text: Expresses an opinion on whether the subject matter conforms to the identified criteria, based on the agreed-upon procedures performed
Expresses a negative-assurance conclusion that nothing came to their attention indicating any noncompliance
Provides reasonable assurance about the overall reliability of the subject matter, but only for the procedures agreed upon

Performs only the specific procedures agreed upon with the engaging party and specified parties, reports the factual findings from those procedures without expressing any conclusion, and issues a restricted-use report

explanations.a: An AUP engagement does not result in an opinion — that level of assurance characterizes an examination (AT-C 205). The practitioner reports findings only; users draw their own conclusions from the factual results.
explanations.b: A negative-assurance conclusion ('nothing came to our attention') characterizes an attestation review (AT-C 210) or a SSARS financial statement review. An AUP engagement provides no assurance whatsoever — not even limited assurance.
explanations.c: An AUP engagement provides no assurance at any level — not reasonable, limited, or partial. The practitioner takes no responsibility for the sufficiency or completeness of the procedures for any purpose; that responsibility belongs to the engaging party.
explanations.d: AT-C Section 215 specifies the defining characteristics of an AUP engagement: (1) procedures designed and agreed upon by the engaging party and specified parties, not the practitioner; (2) the practitioner performs only those specific procedures and reports the factual findings without expressing any opinion, conclusion, or negative assurance; (3) the report is restricted to the specified parties who understand the limited nature of the procedures; and (4) the specified parties are responsible for determining whether the procedures are sufficient for their purposes. This structure makes AUP useful for highly customized, purpose-specific evaluations where the users want specific facts rather than an overall conclusion.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: AUP reports under AT-C Section 215 are typically restricted to specified parties because

answers.text: The specified parties participated in designing the procedures and therefore understand the limited nature, scope, and purpose of the report — unrestricted distribution to parties who did not participate could mislead users about the level of assurance provided
The AICPA prohibits distributing AUP reports to anyone other than the engaging party for confidentiality reasons
AUP reports contain proprietary business information that would harm the entity if publicly disclosed
AUP engagements are only permitted for publicly traded entities where the SEC controls report distribution

explanations.a: AT-C Section 215 restricts AUP reports to specified parties because those parties participated in defining the procedures — they know exactly what was done and what the findings mean in the context they designed. Third parties who did not participate might interpret the report as providing broader assurance than was actually given. Since the procedures were custom-designed for a specific purpose and the practitioner expresses no overall conclusion, the report is meaningful only to parties who understand its context and limitations. Unrestricted distribution could be misleading.
explanations.b: The AICPA does not categorically prohibit distributing AUP reports — the restriction flows from the engagement's structure and the meaningful limitations of AUP findings, not from a blanket confidentiality rule. The restriction is about preventing misinterpretation, not about organizational secrecy.
explanations.c: While confidentiality of business information may be a practical reason certain parties choose AUP over broader assurance engagements, the fundamental reason for restricting distribution is about the meaningfulness of the report to parties who did not design the procedures.
explanations.d: AUP engagements are available to all types of entities — public, private, nonprofit, governmental — and are not restricted to publicly traded entities. SEC involvement in distribution is not a characteristic of AUP engagements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A practitioner performing an agreed-upon procedures engagement discovers, while performing the agreed procedures, that a significant fraud has likely occurred in an area not covered by the specified procedures. The practitioner's MOST appropriate response is to

answers.text: Immediately expand the procedures beyond those agreed upon to investigate the fraud fully, without notifying the specified parties
Include the fraud finding in the AUP report since the practitioner has a professional duty to communicate all discovered misconduct
Report the fraud directly to law enforcement since it falls outside the scope of the agreed-upon procedures

Communicate the discovery to the appropriate level of the engaging entity (management or those charged with governance) and, if the discovery was within the scope of the agreed procedures, report it as a finding; if outside the scope, consider whether to recommend that additional procedures be performed — but do not unilaterally expand beyond the agreed procedures

explanations.a: The practitioner performing an AUP engagement does not have authority to unilaterally expand procedures beyond those agreed upon. Doing so without notification would change the fundamental nature of the engagement and the agreed-upon scope without the parties' knowledge or consent.
explanations.b: This requires nuance: the AUP report includes findings from the agreed-upon procedures. If the fraud evidence was discovered within the course of performing the agreed procedures (the procedures led the practitioner to uncover it as a finding), it should be reported as a factual finding. However, if the fraud is entirely outside the scope of what the agreed procedures would reveal, the report would not formally include it — but the practitioner would still communicate with appropriate management levels.
explanations.c: Reporting directly to law enforcement is generally not within the practitioner's professional mandate. The practitioner communicates findings to the engaging party and those charged with governance — not directly to law enforcement. Law enforcement reporting by auditors occurs only in specific limited circumstances (e.g., certain regulatory requirements or when the auditor has independent knowledge of crimes against the entity).
explanations.d: This most accurately describes the balanced response. In an AUP engagement, the scope is defined by the agreed-upon procedures. If the practitioner encounters evidence of fraud: (1) If within the procedures performed — report it as a factual finding in the AUP report; (2) If outside the procedures — communicate the matter to the appropriate level of management (or TCWG if management is implicated), suggest that additional procedures may be needed to investigate, and allow the engaging party to decide whether to expand the scope. The practitioner does not unilaterally expand the agreed scope but also does not simply ignore discovered wrongdoing.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A lender and a borrower jointly engage a CPA to perform agreed-upon procedures on the borrower's compliance with specific financial covenants in the loan agreement. The CPA finds that one covenant (minimum current ratio of 1.5:1) is not met — the borrower's current ratio is 1.3:1. How should this finding be reported?

answers.text: The CPA should express a qualified opinion stating that except for the covenant violation, the borrower was compliant with all covenants
The CPA should issue a negative assurance conclusion that except for the current ratio violation, nothing came to their attention indicating noncompliance with other covenants

The CPA should report the factual finding — 'we found the current ratio to be 1.3:1, which does not meet the required minimum of 1.5:1' — along with the results of all other agreed-upon procedures, without expressing an opinion on whether the borrower is compliant or what consequences result from the violation
The CPA should withdraw from the engagement since the discovery of a covenant violation indicates the borrower's financial statements cannot be relied upon

explanations.a: A qualified opinion is appropriate for an examination or audit engagement — not for an AUP engagement. AUP engagements do not produce opinions. Expressing a qualified opinion would mischaracterize the nature of the AUP engagement.
explanations.b: Negative assurance ('nothing came to our attention except...') is the conclusion language for a review engagement — not an AUP engagement. An AUP practitioner does not express any form of conclusion — they report findings only.
explanations.c: This correctly describes AUP reporting. The practitioner's report describes each agreed-upon procedure performed and states the factual finding for each. For the covenant violation: 'We computed the current ratio by dividing current assets by current liabilities as of December 31 and found the current ratio to be 1.3 to 1. The loan agreement requires a minimum current ratio of 1.5 to 1.' The report does not opine on whether this constitutes a covenant violation for legal purposes (that is a legal determination for the parties and their counsel), nor does it express any overall conclusion about compliance. The lender and borrower (who designed the procedures) then interpret the finding in light of the covenant terms.
explanations.d: A covenant violation does not indicate that the financial statements are unreliable — it indicates that the entity failed to meet a specific financial ratio requirement. Covenant violations are common business events that do not automatically impair the reliability of financial information. Withdrawal would be inappropriate in these circumstances.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: Under AR-C Section 70, a preparation engagement is BEST described as one in which

answers.text: The CPA assists management in preparing financial statements without providing any assurance — no CPA report is issued, but each page of the financial statements must include a legend stating 'no assurance is provided'
The CPA performs limited procedures and issues a brief report stating that no misstatements were found during the preparation process
The CPA takes full responsibility for the accuracy of the financial statements since the CPA prepared them
The CPA prepares financial statements from underlying records and issues an audit opinion confirming their accuracy

explanations.a: AR-C Section 70 defines a preparation engagement as an engagement in which the CPA is engaged to prepare financial statements (or assist management in preparing financial statements). Key features: (1) No CPA report is issued — unlike compilations and reviews, preparation does not result in a practitioner's report attached to the financial statements; (2) Each page of the prepared financial statements must include a legend stating that no assurance is provided by the CPA (or equivalent language) — this alerts users to the absence of CPA assurance while acknowledging the CPA's involvement in preparation; (3) Management remains responsible for the financial statements.
explanations.b: A preparation engagement does not involve limited procedures testing, and no report is issued. The CPA does not issue any conclusion or statement about whether misstatements were found — the work product is the financial statements themselves with the no-assurance legend.
explanations.c: Management retains responsibility for the financial statements even when a CPA assists in their preparation. Responsibility does not transfer to the CPA in a preparation engagement — this is an important characteristic that distinguishes preparation from taking over the financial reporting function.
explanations.d: A preparation engagement does not include an audit opinion — in fact, it explicitly provides no assurance. The audit opinion requires GAAS procedures that are far beyond the scope of a preparation engagement.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: Unlike compilation and review engagements, a CPA performing a preparation engagement is NOT required to

answers.text: Communicate the engagement terms in an engagement letter
Understand the entity's applicable financial reporting framework
Prepare financial statements that are appropriate in form for the framework applied
Be independent of the entity for whom the financial statements are prepared

explanations.a: AR-C Section 70 requires the CPA to establish an understanding with management regarding the terms of the preparation engagement, typically through an engagement letter. While the nature of this understanding may be simpler than for a compilation or review, communication of the terms is still required.
explanations.b: To prepare financial statements, the CPA must understand the applicable financial reporting framework — whether GAAP, tax basis, or another special purpose framework — in order to structure the statements appropriately. This understanding is a practical prerequisite for doing the work, even if not framed as a formal requirement in the same way as audits.
explanations.c: Preparing financial statements in the appropriate form for the framework is a core component of the preparation service — the financial statements must follow the format and classification requirements of the applicable framework.
explanations.d: Independence is not required for a preparation engagement. Because preparation does not involve any assurance (the practitioner does not assess, verify, or express a conclusion about the financial statements), the independence requirement that applies to review and audit engagements is not applicable. A CPA who has a financial interest in the client or other independence-impairing relationship may still perform a preparation engagement — though they would need to recuse from higher-assurance services for that client.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A CPA prepares financial statements for a client under AR-C Section 70. The client will use the financial statements to apply for a bank loan. The bank expects to rely on the financial statements in evaluating the loan application. What is the MOST important step the CPA should take?

answers.text: Upgrade the engagement to a compilation so that a CPA report is associated with the financial statements provided to the bank
Include the legend 'no assurance is provided' on each page of the financial statements to ensure that the bank is alerted to the absence of CPA assurance
Issue a letter to the bank confirming the accuracy of the financial statements so that the bank can rely on them
Nothing specific — the CPA's preparation of the financial statements is sufficient for bank loan purposes

explanations.a: Upgrading to a compilation is one option — but AR-C Section 70 does not require a CPA to upgrade the engagement simply because the financial statements will be used by a third party. If the client and CPA agreed on a preparation engagement, the mandatory legend requirement addresses the disclosure obligation for third-party use.
explanations.b: AR-C Section 70 requires the CPA to include a legend on each page of the prepared financial statements stating 'no assurance is provided' (or equivalent language). When financial statements prepared under AR-C 70 will be used by a third party (such as a bank), the legend is the mechanism that alerts users to the absence of CPA assurance — preventing them from relying on the statements as if they had been compiled, reviewed, or audited. The legend is not optional when third parties will use the financial statements.
explanations.c: The CPA cannot issue a letter confirming accuracy — that would constitute a form of assurance (attestation) beyond the scope of a preparation engagement. Issuing such a letter would require the CPA to perform at minimum a compilation engagement.
explanations.d: Simply preparing the financial statements without any indication of the CPA's role or the absence of assurance would mislead the bank. The preparation engagement requires the no-assurance legend specifically to address situations where third parties may see the financial statements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: Under AR-C Section 70, the legend 'no assurance is provided' may be omitted from prepared financial statements only if

answers.text: The client has agreed in the engagement letter to waive the legend requirement
The CPA is also licensed as an attorney and the financial statements are used for legal proceedings
The CPA reasonably expects that the prepared financial statements will not be used by a third party — for example, when they are prepared solely for the entity's internal management use
The financial statements are prepared on a cash basis rather than GAAP — special purpose frameworks do not require the legend

explanations.a: Management's agreement in the engagement letter cannot waive the legend requirement — the standard's purpose is to protect third-party users who will see the financial statements. The CPA cannot contractually eliminate a disclosure requirement designed for user protection simply because the client prefers it.
explanations.b: There is no attorney-CPA exception or legal proceeding exception to the legend requirement. The CPA's professional licensure in another field does not affect the SSARS requirements governing the preparation engagement.
explanations.c: AR-C Section 70 provides that the legend 'no assurance is provided' may be omitted when the CPA reasonably expects that the financial statements will not be used by a third party. If the statements are prepared solely for the entity's internal management use — for example, for internal budgeting, management decision-making, or internal performance evaluation — and will not be shared with banks, investors, or other external parties, the rationale for the legend (alerting third parties) does not apply. The CPA must use professional judgment about whether third-party use is reasonably expected.
explanations.d: The framework (GAAP vs. cash basis vs. other special purpose) does not determine whether the legend is required. The legend requirement applies to all preparation engagements regardless of the financial reporting framework used — it relates to the nature of the service (no assurance), not to the accounting framework.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A compilation engagement under AR-C Section 80 MOST accurately provides

answers.text: Reasonable assurance that the financial statements are free of material misstatement
Limited assurance based on inquiries and analytical procedures
No assurance — the CPA assists management in presenting financial information in the form of financial statements but does not verify, corroborate, or test the accuracy of the information provided
Absolute assurance through a complete examination of all underlying accounting records

explanations.a: Reasonable assurance characterizes a financial statement audit (or attestation examination) — not a compilation. A compilation requires significantly less work and provides significantly less assurance.
explanations.b: Limited assurance based on inquiries and analytical procedures characterizes a SSARS review engagement (AR-C Section 90) — not a compilation. The review requires more work than a compilation and provides a higher level of assurance.
explanations.c: AR-C Section 80 specifies that a compilation provides no assurance. The CPA performing a compilation: assists management in presenting financial information in the form of financial statements; reads the compiled financial statements and considers whether they appear appropriate in form and free from obvious material errors; and issues a compilation report — but does not verify the accuracy or completeness of the information provided by management, does not test underlying accounting records, and does not perform inquiries to evaluate accounting policies. The compilation report explicitly states that no assurance is provided.
explanations.d: Absolute assurance through complete examination is not a standard professional engagement — it does not exist as an option. No service provides absolute assurance on financial statements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: When a CPA compiling financial statements is NOT independent of the client, the CPA must

answers.text: Decline the compilation engagement since independence is required for all CPA services involving financial statements
Disclose the lack of independence in the compilation report — stating that the CPA is not independent — without being required to state the reason for the lack of independence
Disclose both the lack of independence and the specific reason for the lack of independence in the compilation report
Perform a review instead since reviews provide more assurance and independence is only required for review engagements

explanations.a: Independence is not required for compilation engagements — the compilation provides no assurance, so the independence requirement that applies to assurance engagements does not apply. A CPA may compile financial statements for a client in which the CPA has a financial interest, as long as the lack of independence is disclosed.
explanations.b: AR-C Section 80 allows a CPA who lacks independence to perform a compilation engagement — but requires the CPA to include a separate paragraph in the compilation report indicating that the CPA is not independent with respect to the entity. The standard does not require the CPA to disclose the specific reason for the lack of independence (e.g., 'because I own stock in the entity' or 'because my spouse is the CFO'). However, the CPA may choose to disclose the specific reason.
explanations.c: Disclosing both the fact and the specific reason for lack of independence is one option — AR-C 80 allows the CPA to include additional information — but the standard only requires disclosure of the fact of non-independence, not the reason.
explanations.d: Performing a review requires independence — a CPA who lacks independence cannot perform a SSARS review engagement. Upgrading to a review would not solve the independence problem; it would make the engagement impermissible.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: During a compilation engagement, the CPA's responsibility for reading the compiled financial statements requires the CPA to

answers.text: Read the financial statements and consider whether they appear appropriate in form and free from obvious material errors — while remaining alert to information that appears to be incorrect, incomplete, or otherwise unsatisfactory
Test a sample of the underlying transactions to verify the accuracy of the amounts presented
Perform analytical procedures to identify unusual fluctuations that may indicate potential misstatement
Confirm major account balances with third parties to ensure the financial statements are materially accurate

explanations.a: AR-C Section 80 requires the CPA to read the compiled financial statements and consider whether they appear appropriate in form and free from obvious material errors. This is a relatively limited responsibility — the CPA reads and considers (not tests or verifies) whether the statements look appropriate based on the information provided by management. The CPA should be alert to obvious errors (mathematical mistakes, misclassifications, or disclosures that appear clearly incorrect) but does not independently evaluate the accuracy of the underlying data.
explanations.b: Testing underlying transactions is an audit procedure — far beyond the scope of a compilation engagement. The CPA performing a compilation does not test or corroborate the information provided by management.
explanations.c: Analytical procedures are a characteristic of a review engagement (AR-C 90), where they are performed to identify unusual relationships that may indicate material misstatements. In a compilation, the CPA reads the statements but does not perform structured analytical procedures designed to identify irregularities.
explanations.d: Third-party confirmation of account balances is an audit procedure under AU-C 505. Compilations do not include any procedures to independently verify or corroborate balances — the CPA relies on information provided by management.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: While compiling financial statements for a client, the CPA discovers that the entity has not recorded depreciation for any fixed assets during the current year — the controller explains that the company intends to 'catch up' in the following year. The omission is material. Management declines to correct the departure from GAAP. The CPA's MOST appropriate response is to

answers.text: Issue the compilation report with an unmodified conclusion since the CPA's role is to present financial information, not to ensure compliance with GAAP
Immediately withdraw from the engagement without any further communication since a known GAAP departure invalidates the compilation

Issue the compilation report with an additional paragraph that describes the departure from GAAP (the omission of depreciation) and, if practicable, its effects — or if the CPA concludes the departure is so material that the financial statements are misleading, consider withdrawing
Record the depreciation on behalf of management without their authorization to bring the financial statements into conformity with GAAP

explanations.a: Issuing a compilation report without disclosing a known material departure from GAAP would mislead users. While a compilation does not involve testing or verifying accounting policies, when the CPA becomes aware of a known GAAP departure, AR-C Section 80 requires action — the CPA cannot simply present materially misstated financial statements without disclosure.
explanations.b: Immediate withdrawal without any communication or attempt to resolve the matter is not the required first step. AR-C 80 allows compilations to include departures from GAAP — with appropriate disclosure — in some circumstances. Withdrawal is appropriate if the CPA concludes the departure makes the financial statements so misleading that adding a disclosure paragraph would be insufficient.
explanations.c: AR-C Section 80 addresses known departures from the applicable framework. When management declines to correct a departure, the CPA should: (1) communicate the departure to management and request correction; (2) if management refuses, consider whether to modify the compilation report by adding a paragraph that describes the nature of the departure and, if known, the approximate amount by which each affected line item differs from GAAP; (3) if the departure is so material that the financial statements are misleading even with the disclosure paragraph, the CPA should consider withdrawing from the engagement. The compilation with a departure disclosure paragraph is the middle-ground option that allows the engagement to continue with transparency about the known GAAP departure.
explanations.d: The CPA cannot unilaterally record accounting entries without management's authorization — management is responsible for the financial statements, and the CPA cannot override management's accounting decisions in a compilation engagement. Recording depreciation without authorization would constitute improperly assuming a management function.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: The audit procedures performed in a SSARS review engagement under AR-C Section 90 consist primarily of

answers.text: Physical inspection of assets, third-party confirmation, and recalculation of all significant account balances
Tests of controls over the financial reporting process and detailed vouching of transactions
Analytical procedures applied to financial data and inquiries directed to management and others within the entity about the accounting policies, practices, and financial statement amounts
Observation of physical inventory counts and confirmation of accounts receivable from all significant customers

explanations.a: Physical inspection, third-party confirmation, and recalculation are audit procedures that go well beyond the scope of a SSARS review. These corroborative procedures are what distinguish an audit from a review — the review specifically does not perform these tests.
explanations.b: Tests of controls are audit procedures used in a financial statement audit when the auditor intends to rely on controls. SSARS reviews do not include tests of controls — they are based on a limited set of procedures that provide less evidence than an audit.
explanations.c: AR-C Section 90 specifies that a review consists primarily of: (1) Analytical procedures — comparing financial data to prior periods, expected trends, budgets, and inter-account relationships to identify unusual fluctuations that may indicate potential misstatements; and (2) Inquiries — directed to management (and others within the entity who may have relevant knowledge) about the accounting policies used, whether the financial statements have been prepared in conformity with the framework, and explanations for unexpected relationships identified by analytics. These two procedures distinguish the review from both an audit (more evidence) and a compilation (less).
explanations.d: Observation of physical inventory counts and confirmation of accounts receivable are specific audit evidence-gathering procedures required in certain circumstances by AU-C 501 and 505 respectively. These are corroborative techniques that go beyond the inquiries and analytics of a review engagement.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: The standard conclusion paragraph in a SSARS review report is expressed in which form?

answers.text: In positive form — stating that the financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable framework

In a negative (limited) assurance form — stating that based on the review, the CPA is not aware of any material modifications that should be made to the financial statements for them to be in accordance with the applicable framework
In factual form — describing the results of each procedure performed without expressing any overall conclusion
In absolute form — certifying that the financial statements are accurate and complete

explanations.a: A positive-form conclusion ('the financial statements present fairly, in all material respects') is the language of an unmodified audit opinion — which requires reasonable assurance based on a full audit. A review provides only limited assurance and uses negative-form conclusion language.
explanations.b: AR-C Section 90 specifies that the review report includes a conclusion paragraph in negative (limited assurance) form: 'Based on our review, we are not aware of any material modifications that should be made to the accompanying financial statements for them to be in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America.' This negative form expresses the limited nature of the assurance — the CPA is not affirmatively stating the statements are correct; rather, nothing came to their attention indicating material misstatement.
explanations.c: Reporting only factual results without an overall conclusion describes an agreed-upon procedures report — not a review. A review concludes with a conclusion statement that summarizes the overall assessment based on the procedures performed.
explanations.d: Absolute form certification does not exist as a standard professional conclusion — no engagement provides absolute certainty. The review's negative-form conclusion is specifically designed to reflect the limited nature of the evidence gathered.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: The PRIMARY difference between a SSARS review engagement and a financial statement audit is

answers.text: A review can only be performed for privately held companies while an audit can be performed for any entity type
A review requires independence while an audit does not
A review uses sampling while an audit tests every transaction in the population

A review provides limited assurance based primarily on inquiries and analytics, resulting in a negative-form conclusion — while an audit provides reasonable assurance based on more extensive evidence gathering, resulting in a positive-form opinion

explanations.a: SSARS reviews are available for privately held companies — they are not available for issuers subject to SEC reporting (who must have audits and, if interim, PCAOB reviews). However, the primary difference between a review and an audit is not entity type — it is the level of assurance and procedures.
explanations.b: Both reviews and audits require the CPA to be independent. Independence is a prerequisite for both services — the difference lies in the procedures performed and the level of assurance provided, not in the independence requirement.
explanations.c: Both reviews and audits may use sampling techniques in certain procedures. An audit does not test every transaction — it uses risk-based sampling. The difference is not about sampling methodology but about the overall depth of the evidence-gathering process.
explanations.d: The fundamental distinction is the level of assurance and the evidence base: (1) A SSARS review (AR-C 90) provides limited assurance through inquiries and analytical procedures — procedures that do not corroborate management's information with independent evidence. The conclusion is expressed negatively ('we are not aware of any material modifications'); (2) A financial statement audit (GAAS) provides reasonable assurance through a comprehensive set of procedures including tests of controls, substantive testing, confirmation, inspection, and recalculation. The opinion is expressed positively ('the financial statements present fairly'). The difference in evidence depth produces the difference in assurance level and conclusion form.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: During a SSARS review, the CPA identifies that inventory appears to be significantly overvalued — management's year-end inventory balance is 35% higher than what the analytical procedures would predict based on units sold and historical margins. Management declines to adjust the inventory balance or provide a satisfactory explanation. The CPA's MOST appropriate response is to

answers.text: Issue the review report with the standard unmodified conclusion since the CPA cannot verify inventory amounts without performing an audit

Issue a modified review conclusion — disclosing the departure from the framework and describing its known or estimated financial effects, or if the departure is so significant that the financial statements are misleading, consider withdrawing from the engagement
Perform additional audit-level procedures to confirm or deny the inventory overstatement before issuing the review report
Upgrade the engagement to a compilation since compilation does not require disclosure of known GAAP departures in all circumstances

explanations.a: Issuing an unmodified conclusion while aware of a probable material misstatement that management refuses to correct is not appropriate. The unmodified conclusion would state the CPA is not aware of material modifications needed — which would be inaccurate if the CPA has analytical evidence suggesting material overstatement.
explanations.b: AR-C Section 90 addresses situations where the CPA believes material modifications should be made. If management does not make the required modifications, the CPA should: (1) describe the departure (inventory appears overstated based on analytical evidence) and its estimated effect on the financial statements in the review report; (2) modify the review conclusion to note that, except for the described departure, the CPA is not aware of any other material modifications needed; or (3) if the departure is so pervasive that the financial statements are misleading, consider whether withdrawing is appropriate.
explanations.c: Performing audit-level procedures would change the fundamental nature of the engagement from a review to an audit — which would require a different engagement agreement, independence assessment, and work scope. The SSARS framework does not contemplate escalating to audit procedures within a review engagement when a possible misstatement is identified.
explanations.d: Downgrading to a compilation after performing review procedures is not standard practice — and the reason given (avoiding disclosure obligations) would be inappropriate. If the CPA has obtained information through review procedures suggesting material overstatement, that information cannot simply be forgotten or ignored by changing the engagement level.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: During a SSARS review, the CPA's inquiries reveal that the entity changed its revenue recognition methodology during the year in a manner that appears inconsistent with the applicable framework, but management refuses to provide documentation supporting the change. The CPA cannot perform the necessary procedures to evaluate the accounting policy change. Which response MOST appropriately addresses this situation?

answers.text: Issue the review report with the standard unmodified conclusion and note the revenue recognition change as an emphasis-of-matter paragraph
Modify the review conclusion to a qualified conclusion — except for the revenue recognition matter — and continue with the engagement

Assess whether the inability to perform the necessary procedures constitutes a limitation in the scope of the review that may require the CPA to consider withdrawing from the engagement rather than issuing a review report that could be misleading
Perform a compilation instead, since compilation does not require evaluation of accounting policy changes

explanations.a: An unmodified conclusion when the CPA cannot complete the necessary procedures to evaluate a material accounting policy change is inappropriate. The unmodified conclusion implies the CPA is not aware of material modifications needed — but if the CPA cannot evaluate the revenue recognition policy, they cannot make this representation.
explanations.b: A 'qualified' review conclusion ('except for the revenue recognition matter, we are not aware of...') is not a standard form of review report modification. Review reports are modified by either (1) describing a known departure from the framework, or (2) withdrawing — there is no direct equivalent of an audit 'except for scope limitation' in the SSARS review framework.
explanations.c: AR-C Section 90 provides guidance when the CPA cannot perform the procedures necessary for a review. If the scope of the review is limited to the point where the CPA cannot obtain the evidence needed to complete the review procedures and form a meaningful conclusion, the CPA should consider whether continuing is appropriate. Unlike an audit where scope limitations can result in a qualified opinion or disclaimer, the SSARS framework generally does not contemplate a limited-scope review conclusion — the more appropriate response to scope limitations that prevent completing the review is withdrawal with communication of the reasons.
explanations.d: Downgrading to a compilation to avoid the scope issue is not appropriate. The CPA cannot use the compilation framework as a mechanism to sidestep evaluation obligations encountered during a review. Additionally, if the CPA has already obtained information through review procedures suggesting a material departure, that information cannot be ignored by changing engagement level.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A CPA performs a SSARS review of Granite Corp's current-year financial statements. The prior-year comparative financial statements (included for comparison) were reviewed by a different firm, which issued an unmodified review conclusion. During the current-year review, the CPA identifies information suggesting the prior-year inventory was materially overstated — the prior CPA firm's review may have been inadequate. How should the current-year CPA address this situation?

answers.text: Disregard the prior-year information since the current CPA's responsibility is limited to the current-year statements

The current-year CPA should consider the implications for the current-year review and the comparative statements — if the prior-year misstatement affected beginning balances that flow into current-year results, additional procedures may be needed; the CPA should communicate the matter to management and consider whether the comparative statements need to be restated and whether the current-year report should address the prior-year information
Issue a current-year review report with an adverse conclusion since the prior-year comparative statements are materially misstated
Immediately contact the prior firm to demand they revise their review report before the current-year report can be issued

explanations.a: The current-year CPA cannot simply disregard prior-year information in comparative financial statements. When prior-year statements are included for comparison and the current-year CPA identifies evidence of material misstatement in those statements, the situation has implications for both the comparative statements and potentially for the current year (through beginning balances).
explanations.b: This describes the most appropriate professional response. If the prior-year inventory was materially overstated, the current-year beginning inventory (and therefore cost of goods sold and gross margin) may also be misstated — creating a direct link to the current-year statements the CPA is reviewing. The CPA should: (1) evaluate whether the beginning balance error affects current-year results; (2) perform additional procedures as needed to assess the current-year impact; (3) communicate the matter to management (and TCWG) regarding both the prior-year misstatement and its implications; (4) consider whether the comparative financial statements need to be restated — management is responsible for the revision; and (5) evaluate the appropriate reporting approach for the current-year review, which may include an other-matter paragraph if the comparative statements are revised or were not reviewed by the current CPA.
explanations.c: An adverse conclusion in a SSARS review would be issued for a pervasive departure from the applicable framework affecting the current-year statements. A prior-year misstatement in comparative statements does not automatically trigger an adverse conclusion on current-year statements — it requires evaluation of its specific effects on the current period.
explanations.d: The current-year CPA cannot compel the prior firm to revise its report. The prior firm's responsibilities are governed by its engagement with the client and its own professional standards — the current-year CPA can communicate with management and TCWG, but does not have authority over the prior firm. If the prior-year statements need to be revised, that is a management and client decision.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: In a compliance audit (as distinct from a financial statement audit), the primary objective is to

answers.text: Express an opinion on whether the entity's financial statements are fairly presented in accordance with GAAP
Express an opinion or conclusion on whether the entity has complied with specific laws, regulations, contracts, or grant requirements identified as the compliance subject matter
Test the design of internal controls to identify potential risks to the entity's operations
Evaluate the efficiency and effectiveness of the entity's operational programs and management practices

explanations.a: Expressing an opinion on fair presentation of financial statements is the objective of a financial statement audit — not a compliance audit. While some compliance audits are integrated with financial statement audits (such as single audits), a compliance audit has compliance as its primary focus.
explanations.b: A compliance audit (governed by AU-C 935, or specific regulatory frameworks such as the Uniform Guidance for single audits) provides assurance about whether the entity has complied with the specified compliance requirements. The subject matter — the compliance requirements — is defined in advance (e.g., federal grant requirements, environmental regulations, loan covenants), and the auditor evaluates whether the entity's activities and expenditures conformed to those requirements.
explanations.c: Testing control design is part of understanding internal controls — it is an element of risk assessment in both financial statement and compliance audits. It is not itself the primary objective of a compliance audit.
explanations.d: Evaluating program efficiency and effectiveness describes performance auditing — a distinct type of engagement available under Government Auditing Standards (GAGAS). Performance auditing addresses 'economy, efficiency, and effectiveness' questions — not compliance with specified requirements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: Under Government Auditing Standards (Yellow Book), an auditor of a governmental entity's financial statements must issue which additional report(s) beyond the standard financial statement audit opinion?

answers.text: A report on the entity's compliance with its strategic plan and key performance indicators
A report on the operating efficiency of the entity's major programs and services
A report on fraud detected during the audit, submitted directly to the state legislature

A report on internal control over financial reporting and a report on compliance with applicable laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements that could have a direct and material effect on the financial statements

explanations.a: Compliance with strategic plans and key performance indicators is not a standard GAGAS reporting requirement — performance auditing may address these matters in a separate performance audit engagement, but the standard GAGAS financial audit report package does not include a strategic plan compliance report.
explanations.b: Operating efficiency of programs is the subject of a performance audit under GAGAS — a separate engagement type from the financial statement audit. The standard GAGAS financial audit reporting package addresses internal control and compliance, not operational efficiency.
explanations.c: GAGAS does not require auditors to submit a separate fraud report directly to the state legislature. Fraud findings are communicated through the compliance and internal control reports and through direct communication with management and TCWG. The audit report package is transmitted to management and oversight bodies — not as a direct legislature submission bypassing management.
explanations.d: GAGAS paragraph 6.10 requires that when performing a financial audit in accordance with Government Auditing Standards, the auditor must issue: (1) a report on internal control over financial reporting — describing significant deficiencies and material weaknesses identified; and (2) a report on compliance with applicable laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements that could have a direct and material effect on the financial statements. These reports are in addition to (and typically issued alongside) the standard financial statement audit opinion.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: In a single audit performed under the Uniform Guidance, what type of compliance opinion does the auditor issue for each major federal program?

answers.text: An opinion on whether the entity complied, in all material respects, with the types of compliance requirements applicable to each major federal program
A negative assurance conclusion that nothing came to the auditor's attention indicating noncompliance with major program requirements
A disclaimer of opinion since the Uniform Guidance does not require the auditor to express a compliance opinion — only to report findings in the Schedule of Findings
An advisory report on best practices for improving compliance with the federal program requirements, without an assurance conclusion

explanations.a: AU-C Section 935 and the Uniform Guidance (2 CFR § 200.514) require the auditor to express an opinion on compliance for each major federal program. The opinion states whether the entity complied, in all material respects, with the types of compliance requirements applicable to each major program — a positive-form opinion (or a qualified, adverse, or disclaimer if warranted). This is a compliance audit opinion — distinct from the financial statement audit opinion and the internal control reports.
explanations.b: Negative assurance conclusions characterize attestation reviews and certain other lower-assurance engagements. The single audit compliance opinion is a positive-form opinion (or modified if warranted) — not negative assurance. The higher evidence standard of a compliance audit supports a positive-form conclusion.
explanations.c: A compliance opinion is expressly required in a single audit — it is not optional. The Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs is an additional reporting requirement, not a substitute for the compliance opinion.
explanations.d: Advisory reports on best practices are management consulting — not an audit or attestation service. The single audit requires independent assurance (a compliance opinion), not advisory recommendations.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A bank engages a CPA to perform agreed-upon procedures on whether a borrower has complied with the financial covenants in the loan agreement. What type of report does the CPA issue, and what level of assurance is provided?

answers.text: An audit opinion on covenant compliance, providing reasonable assurance that all covenants were met
A review conclusion on covenant compliance, providing limited assurance based on inquiries and analytics
