An agreed-upon procedures report that describes the procedures performed and the factual findings for each covenant tested — without expressing any opinion, conclusion, or level of assurance on compliance
A management letter to the bank describing the auditor's qualitative assessment of whether the borrower is a good credit risk

explanations.a: An audit opinion on covenant compliance would require a compliance audit (AU-C 935) — not an agreed-upon procedures engagement. AUP engagements provide no assurance; they report findings only.
explanations.b: A review conclusion with limited assurance would be appropriate for an attestation review (AT-C 210) on compliance — not for an agreed-upon procedures engagement. AUP engagements provide no assurance whatsoever.
explanations.c: An agreed-upon procedures report on loan covenant compliance describes each procedure performed (e.g., 'We computed the current ratio by dividing current assets... We found the current ratio to be 1.4:1') and the finding for each covenant tested, without expressing any overall opinion or conclusion on whether the entity was 'compliant' with the loan agreement. The bank and borrower — who designed the procedures — draw their own conclusions from the specific findings. This is the typical structure for covenant compliance AUP engagements.
explanations.d: A management letter describing the auditor's qualitative credit assessment is a consulting service — not an assurance or agreed-upon procedures engagement. This would not be appropriate in response to the bank's request for evidence about covenant compliance.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: An auditor conducting a financial statement audit under GAAS discovers that the entity violated a tax law during the year, resulting in a $2 million penalty that was not recorded. The penalty is material to the financial statements. How does this compliance violation MOST directly affect the financial statement audit report?

answers.text: The financial statement audit report is unaffected since tax law violations are addressed in a separate compliance report, not the financial statement opinion
The financial statement audit report must be qualified because all tax compliance violations require an 'except for' opinion
The financial statement audit report is not directly affected since penalties are disclosed only in the notes — they do not affect the balance sheet

If management does not record the unrecorded $2 million penalty, the financial statements contain a material misstatement — the auditor's opinion should be modified (qualified or adverse, depending on pervasiveness) if management refuses to correct the error, since compliance violations that result in unrecorded material liabilities directly affect the fairness of the financial statements

explanations.a: While tax violations that do not affect financial statement amounts may be addressed separately (e.g., in a GAGAS compliance report), a violation that results in a material unrecorded liability directly affects the financial statements — and therefore directly affects the audit opinion on those financial statements.
explanations.b: Not all tax compliance violations require a qualified opinion — only those that result in material financial statement misstatements. A technical tax violation with immaterial financial consequences would not affect the opinion. A blanket 'all violations require qualification' rule does not reflect auditing standards.
explanations.c: A $2 million penalty that should have been recorded but was not is a balance sheet item — it represents an unrecorded liability (accounts payable — taxes and penalties). The statement that penalties 'do not affect the balance sheet' is incorrect. An unrecorded liability is a balance sheet misstatement.
explanations.d: The connection between the compliance violation and the financial statements is the unrecorded $2 million penalty. Under GAAP, a probable and estimable loss contingency (including a tax penalty) must be accrued (ASC 450). If management refuses to record the liability: (1) accounts payable or accrued liabilities are understated by $2 million; (2) the income statement lacks the penalty expense; (3) the financial statements are materially misstated. The auditor must evaluate whether the misstatement is material and pervasive — if material but not pervasive, a qualified opinion; if material and pervasive, an adverse opinion.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A GAGAS audit of a county government reveals: (1) a material weakness in ICFR related to the authorization of capital expenditures; (2) instances of noncompliance with the county's purchasing ordinance for three procurement transactions (totaling $380,000) that appear intentional; and (3) no material misstatement in the financial statements — the financial statements present fairly. Which combination of reports and conclusions is MOST appropriate for this engagement?

answers.text: Issue only one report — an adverse opinion on the financial statements — since a material weakness automatically means the financial statements are not fairly presented
Issue an unmodified financial statement opinion, an adverse ICFR opinion, and an unmodified compliance opinion — since the compliance violations were not material to the financial statements
Issue no reports until the county corrects all identified deficiencies and noncompliance — GAGAS does not allow issuance of reports when significant findings exist

Issue an unmodified financial statement opinion (the statements are fairly presented), a report on internal control identifying the material weakness (and its nature), and a report on compliance that either modifies the compliance conclusion or describes the noncompliance instances — since they appear intentional and material to the compliance report even if not to the financial statements

explanations.a: A material weakness in ICFR does not automatically make financial statements materially misstated. The material weakness indicates a risk of undetected misstatement — but if audit procedures provide sufficient evidence that the financial statements are fairly presented despite the weakness, the financial statement opinion can be unmodified. A material weakness and financial statement opinion are separate evaluations.
explanations.b: In an integrated GAGAS audit, the ICFR report identifies and describes significant deficiencies and material weaknesses — but unlike the PCAOB integrated audit, GAGAS does not typically result in a separate adverse or unmodified opinion on ICFR effectiveness in the same way as a SOX 404(b) integrated audit. The GAGAS ICFR report describes the identified deficiencies. Additionally, the compliance violations appear intentional and are material to the compliance evaluation — characterizing the compliance report as 'unmodified' would not accurately reflect the findings.
explanations.c: GAGAS requires issuance of reports regardless of whether findings exist — the reports communicate both the auditor's conclusions and any identified issues. Withholding reports pending remediation is not within the auditor's authority.
explanations.d: This is the most accurate description: (1) Financial statement opinion — unmodified, because the audit determined the financial statements present fairly despite the material weakness (audit procedures provided sufficient evidence of fair presentation); (2) Internal control report — identifies the material weakness in capital expenditure authorization, describes its nature, and potentially evaluates its implications; (3) Compliance report — because the three procurement violations appear intentional (suggesting more than accidental noncompliance) and total $380,000 (material to the compliance evaluation), the compliance report would either be modified to describe the material noncompliance or, at minimum, identify the violations as significant findings. GAGAS requires this type of comprehensive, transparent reporting even when the financial statements themselves are fairly presented.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: When an auditor provides a report on an entity's compliance with aspects of contractual agreements or regulatory requirements based on an audit of financial statements, the assurance expressed is

answers.text: Reasonable assurance — the compliance report is equivalent in assurance level to the financial statement opinion
Negative assurance — the auditor states that nothing came to their attention indicating the entity failed to comply with the specified provisions tested during the audit
No assurance — the compliance report is informational only and makes no statement about the entity's compliance
Absolute assurance — because the compliance provisions are specific and objectively verifiable

explanations.a: Compliance reporting based on an audit of financial statements provides negative (limited) assurance, not the reasonable assurance of the financial statement opinion itself. The distinction is important: the audit provides reasonable assurance about the financial statements; the compliance report based on that audit provides only negative assurance because compliance procedures are not as extensive as the financial statement audit procedures.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 806 specifies that when an auditor reports on compliance with aspects of contractual agreements or regulatory requirements in connection with an audit of financial statements, the report expresses negative assurance — stating that nothing came to the auditor's attention indicating noncompliance with the specified provisions. This lower level of assurance reflects that compliance was not audited to the same depth as the financial statements.
explanations.c: A compliance report based on an audit does provide assurance — specifically negative (limited) assurance. It is not merely informational without any assurance content.
explanations.d: Absolute assurance is unattainable in any professional engagement. Even compliance reports with objectively verifiable provisions provide only limited (negative) assurance, not absolute assurance.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: Under Government Auditing Standards (Yellow Book), what additional reports must an auditor issue beyond the standard financial statement opinion?

answers.text: A report on internal control over financial reporting and a report on compliance with laws, regulations, and provisions of contracts or grant agreements applicable to the audit
A forensic investigation report and a report on the entity's risk management framework
A management effectiveness report and a report on the entity's strategic planning process
A performance audit report and a report on the effectiveness of internal audit functions

explanations.a: Government Auditing Standards (2018 Yellow Book) require auditors performing financial audits to issue two additional reports alongside the financial statement opinion: (1) a report on internal control over financial reporting — describing significant deficiencies and material weaknesses identified during the audit; and (2) a report on compliance with provisions of laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements applicable to the audited entity — communicating any identified instances of noncompliance. These additional reports fulfill the Yellow Book's public accountability requirements.
explanations.b: Forensic investigation reports and risk management framework assessments are not standard Yellow Book financial audit reporting requirements. Forensic investigations are separately engaged engagements; risk management assessments are management's responsibility.
explanations.c: Management effectiveness reports and strategic planning assessments are management consulting activities, not financial audit reporting requirements under Government Auditing Standards.
explanations.d: Performance audit reports are issued in performance audit engagements (a separate type of engagement under GAGAS) — not as part of the financial audit. Reports on the effectiveness of internal audit functions are not a standard GAGAS financial audit requirement.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: In a single audit, the auditor identifies material noncompliance with an allowable cost requirement for a major federal program — the entity charged $220,000 of unallowable personnel costs to the program. The total program expenditures were $4.5 million. The auditor concludes this noncompliance is material but isolated to this requirement and this program. Which compliance opinion should be issued for this program?

answers.text: A qualified compliance opinion — expressing a conclusion that the entity complied with applicable requirements in all material respects, except for the material noncompliance with the allowable cost requirement described in the report
An adverse compliance opinion because any material noncompliance requires an adverse opinion
An unmodified compliance opinion since $220,000 represents less than 5% of program expenditures and is therefore immaterial
A disclaimer of opinion because the auditor cannot determine the full extent of noncompliance in the program

explanations.a: A qualified compliance opinion uses 'except for' language — expressing that the entity complied with all applicable requirements in all material respects, except for the material noncompliance with the allowable costs requirement. This accurately reflects that the entity complied with other requirements (eligibility, reporting, subrecipient monitoring, etc.) while having a specific identified noncompliance with allowable costs.
explanations.b: An adverse opinion is appropriate when noncompliance is material AND pervasive to the program. Here, the noncompliance is isolated to one compliance requirement (allowable costs) — it does not affect all compliance requirements across the program. An adverse opinion would overstate the scope of the problem.
explanations.c: $220,000 against $4.5 million in program expenditures (approximately 4.9%) may be material to the program's compliance — the auditor has already concluded it is material. Materiality in a compliance context is not determined by a fixed percentage threshold and cannot be dismissed simply because it is below 5%.
explanations.d: A disclaimer of opinion arises from pervasive scope limitations — the inability to obtain sufficient evidence. The auditor has obtained sufficient evidence and has identified a specific noncompliance — the issue is not a scope limitation but a material noncompliance in a specific area.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A compliance audit is performed for a healthcare organization to provide assurance about its compliance with HIPAA privacy requirements. The applicable standard for this engagement is

answers.text: SSAE 18, AT-C Section 205 — an attestation examination engagement, since the auditor is expressing an opinion on subject matter (compliance with HIPAA) against identified criteria (HIPAA regulations)
SSARS AR-C Section 90 — a review engagement, since the compliance testing involves inquiries and analytical procedures
AU-C Section 935 — a compliance audit engagement, since HIPAA is a federal law and all federal law compliance audits must be conducted under AU-C 935
The engagement cannot be performed by a CPA since HIPAA compliance assessment requires a licensed healthcare attorney

explanations.a: A compliance engagement where the practitioner expresses an opinion on whether an entity complied with specified requirements (HIPAA) against defined criteria (the HIPAA Privacy Rule) is an attestation examination engagement under SSAE 18 (AT-C Section 205). The three elements of an attestation engagement are present: the responsible party (the healthcare organization), the subject matter (HIPAA privacy compliance), and suitable criteria (HIPAA regulatory requirements). The practitioner obtains sufficient appropriate evidence and expresses a positive-form opinion.
explanations.b: A review engagement provides limited assurance and results in a negative-form conclusion. If reasonable assurance (positive opinion) on HIPAA compliance is needed, an examination — not a review — is the appropriate engagement type.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 935 applies specifically to compliance audits of governmental entities or entities receiving federal financial assistance — it is not the applicable standard for all compliance engagements involving federal laws. A private healthcare organization not receiving federal grants would not conduct its compliance engagement under AU-C 935.
explanations.d: CPAs regularly perform compliance attestation engagements and may assess compliance with laws and regulations including HIPAA. While legal interpretation of complex provisions may require legal counsel, the attestation examination of compliance is within CPAs' professional scope.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: An auditor performing a financial audit under Government Auditing Standards identifies instances of noncompliance with state procurement regulations during the engagement. The noncompliance did not result in material misstatements in the financial statements. Under GAGAS, how should the auditor address this finding?

answers.text: Ignore the noncompliance since it did not result in financial statement misstatements — the GAGAS report only addresses matters that affect the financial statements

Report the noncompliance in the GAGAS compliance report — including a description of the condition, the applicable criteria, the cause, and the potential effect — even though it did not produce a financial statement misstatement
Report the noncompliance to state law enforcement and cease the audit until the matter is resolved
Include the noncompliance as an emphasis-of-matter paragraph in the financial statement opinion report

explanations.a: GAGAS compliance reporting is not limited to noncompliance that affects the financial statements. Government Auditing Standards require reporting of noncompliance with laws, regulations, and contract provisions regardless of whether the noncompliance results in a financial statement misstatement. The GAGAS compliance report has a broader scope than the financial statement audit — it addresses how government entities use their authority and resources.
explanations.b: The Yellow Book (paragraph 6.15) requires auditors to report noncompliance with provisions of laws, regulations, contracts, or grant agreements in the GAGAS compliance report, regardless of whether the noncompliance produced a financial statement misstatement. The finding report must include: condition (what happened), criteria (what was required), cause (why it happened), and effect (actual or potential impact). Procurement regulation violations are specifically within scope since they govern how government funds are spent.
explanations.c: GAGAS auditors do not have law enforcement authority and do not halt audits to await resolution of noncompliance. The finding is documented and reported — law enforcement reporting by the auditor occurs only in specific circumstances defined in GAGAS, such as illegal acts that represent significant criminal activity.
explanations.d: An emphasis-of-matter paragraph in the financial statement opinion addresses matters that are already presented in the financial statements. Noncompliance findings that don't appear in the financial statements are addressed in the GAGAS compliance report — a separate required document — not in an emphasis-of-matter paragraph in the financial statement report.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: When audited financial statements are presented for two years in a comparative format, the auditor's report generally

answers.text: Covers only the most recent year — the prior year is presented for context only and is not subject to the current auditor's opinion
Is limited to the prior year since the current year is still 'in progress' at the time of reporting
Covers both periods presented — the auditor expresses an opinion on the financial statements of both the current year and the comparative prior year
Is required only for public companies — private entities may present comparative statements without audit coverage of the prior year

explanations.a: When the same auditor audits both years and both periods are presented, the auditor's report covers both periods. Presenting comparative statements without covering the prior period in the report would mislead users into thinking prior-year statements had been audited when they may not have been (or vice versa).
explanations.b: The audit report for comparative statements typically covers the current year as the primary period but also addresses the prior year. The report is not limited to prior years — the current-period audit is the primary engagement.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 700 addresses comparative financial statements. When comparative statements are presented and the same auditor audited both periods, the auditor's report includes an opinion on both periods. The current-year report 'updates' the prior-year opinion — meaning the auditor reconsiders the prior-year opinion in light of all currently available information and expresses an updated conclusion for both periods.
explanations.d: The comparative statement reporting requirements apply to both public and private companies. The requirement is not limited to SEC registrants — any entity presenting comparative financial statements must ensure appropriate coverage of both periods presented.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: When an entity changes from one acceptable accounting principle to another (e.g., from FIFO to weighted average inventory costing), and the change is properly disclosed and the cumulative effect is appropriately presented, the auditor should

answers.text: Issue a qualified opinion because any change in accounting principle creates a departure from the prior year's reporting framework
Refuse to issue an opinion until management reverts to the original accounting principle
Include an emphasis-of-matter paragraph in the audit report drawing attention to the change in accounting principle and referring to the relevant note disclosure
Issue the standard unmodified opinion without any additional communication since changes in accounting principle are permitted under GAAP

explanations.a: A change from one acceptable accounting principle to another is not a departure from the framework — both principles are acceptable under GAAP. A change in principle does not result in a qualified opinion when properly presented and disclosed.
explanations.b: Management has the right to change accounting principles as long as the new principle is preferable and the change is properly disclosed and the cumulative effect reflected. The auditor does not require management to revert to a prior principle.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 708 (Consistency of Financial Statements) requires the auditor to include an emphasis-of-matter paragraph when a change in accounting principle has a material effect on comparability of financial statements. The paragraph alerts readers to the change, explains its nature, and refers to the related note disclosure. This does not modify the unmodified opinion — it supplements it to ensure users understand the comparability issue.
explanations.d: While changes in accounting principle are permitted, they require more than just issuing a standard unmodified opinion — the consistency paragraph is required when the change materially affects comparability. The purpose is to alert users that the year-to-year comparison is affected by the change.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: Comparative financial statements include the current year (audited by Green & Associates) and the prior year (audited by the predecessor, Wilson LLP). Wilson LLP has not been engaged to reissue their prior-period report. What must Green & Associates include in their current-year audit report?

answers.text: Green & Associates should audit the prior year as well, since they cannot issue a report covering only the current year when comparative statements are presented
Green & Associates' report need not mention the prior-year statements at all — the prior year is not their responsibility
Green & Associates should modify their opinion to express a qualified conclusion on the current year due to the lack of reissued predecessor report

Green & Associates must indicate in their report that the prior-year financial statements were audited by a predecessor auditor, identify the predecessor, state the type of opinion Wilson LLP expressed, and disclose the date of Wilson LLP's report

explanations.a: Green & Associates is not required to re-audit the prior year simply because comparative statements are presented. The prior year was audited by a predecessor — Green & Associates' responsibility is clearly the current year, with appropriate disclosure about the predecessor's prior-year audit.
explanations.b: Completely ignoring the prior-year statements in the report would be misleading — users would not understand who provided assurance on the prior-year figures presented in the comparative statements. The report must address the prior year's audit coverage.
explanations.c: The absence of a reissued predecessor report does not require Green & Associates to modify their current-year opinion. The prior year's audit was performed by a qualified predecessor — the current auditor's responsibility is to properly disclose this in their report.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 700 requires that when comparative financial statements include a prior period audited by a predecessor auditor who has not reissued their report, the successor (current) auditor's report must: indicate that the prior-period financial statements were audited by a predecessor auditor; state the type of opinion the predecessor expressed; and disclose the date of the predecessor's report. This disclosure ensures users understand who provided assurance on each period presented.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: An auditor issued an unmodified opinion on Year 2 financial statements. During the Year 3 audit, the auditor discovers that the Year 2 financial statements contained a material misstatement that was not detected during the Year 2 audit. Management restates the Year 2 statements. In the Year 3 comparative report, how should the auditor address the restated Year 2 statements?

answers.text: Reissue the original Year 2 report without modification since the auditor performed the procedures correctly and the misstatement was not the auditor's fault
Express a dual-dated report: the original Year 2 date for Year 2 matters and the Year 3 date for the current year — without any reference to the restatement
Withdraw from the engagement since the prior-year misstatement compromises the integrity of the current-year engagement

Update the Year 2 opinion to address the restated financial statements — expressing an updated opinion on the restated Year 2 statements and including an emphasis-of-matter paragraph describing the restatement and referring to the relevant note disclosure

explanations.a: Reissuing the original Year 2 report without modification would imply the original unmodified opinion applies to the restated statements — which now differ from the statements on which the original opinion was based. The auditor must update their opinion to reflect their assessment of the restated statements.
explanations.b: A dual-dated report is used when a subsequent event occurs after the report date. The restated Year 2 statements require an updated (revised) Year 2 opinion that supersedes the original — dual-dating does not appropriately address a restatement.
explanations.c: A prior-year misstatement that has been restated and disclosed does not require withdrawal from the current-year engagement. The restatement addresses the prior misstatement — the auditor continues with the current-year audit and updates the prior-year opinion as part of the comparative report.
explanations.d: When comparative financial statements include a restated prior period, the auditor updates their opinion on the restated prior-period statements. AU-C Section 700 requires the updated report to address the restated financial statements and include an emphasis-of-matter paragraph that: identifies the restatement, refers to the note disclosing the restatement and its effects, and indicates that the opinion on the restated prior-period statements supersedes the previously issued opinion.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: other information in documents containing audited financial statements
questions.text: Under AU-C Section 720, 'other information' in the context of auditing refers to

answers.text: Financial and non-financial information included in a document containing audited financial statements, other than the audited statements and their accompanying notes — such as management's discussion and analysis (MD&A) or the annual report narrative
Information about the entity that the auditor obtains from sources outside the entity during audit planning
Internal communications between the auditor and those charged with governance that are not included in the public audit report
Supplementary information that the entity presents alongside the audited financial statements and that the auditor reports on under AU-C 725

explanations.a: AU-C Section 720 defines 'other information' as financial or non-financial information (other than audited financial statements and the auditor's report) included in a document containing the audited financial statements. This typically includes: the management discussion and analysis (MD&A) section; the annual report's chairman's letter or introduction; five-year financial summaries; information about officers; and other narrative or quantitative content included alongside the audited statements. The other information is not audited, but the auditor reads it to identify material inconsistencies or material misstatements of fact.
explanations.b: Information obtained from external sources during audit planning is audit evidence — not 'other information' in the AU-C 720 sense. The AU-C 720 definition specifically refers to information included in documents containing the audited financial statements.
explanations.c: Internal communications between the auditor and TCWG (such as AU-C 260 communications) are engagement communications — they are not 'other information' under AU-C 720.
explanations.d: Supplementary information under AU-C 725 is a separate category — when the auditor actively reports on supplementary information, it is covered by AU-C 725, not AU-C 720. AU-C 720 'other information' is information for which the auditor reads but does not report on directly.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: other information in documents containing audited financial statements
questions.text: Under AU-C Section 720, the auditor's primary responsibility with respect to other information is to

answers.text: Audit the other information and include the results of that audit in a separate section of the auditor's report
Refuse to allow other information to be included in documents containing audited financial statements
Express an opinion on the other information separate from the financial statement opinion

Read the other information and consider whether it contains a material inconsistency with the audited financial statements or a material misstatement of fact — taking appropriate action if such matters are identified

explanations.a: The auditor does not audit other information under AU-C 720. The obligation is more limited — reading and considering, not auditing. Auditing would require the same level of evidence-gathering applied to the financial statements, which is not what AU-C 720 requires.
explanations.b: The auditor does not have authority to prevent management from including other information in annual reports or other documents. The auditor's role is to read and consider that information — not to control what management includes.
explanations.c: The auditor does not express a separate opinion on other information — they express no conclusion on it at all. The only 'report' on other information occurs if the auditor identifies a material inconsistency that must be communicated.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 720 requires the auditor to: (1) read the other information and (2) consider whether it contains a material inconsistency with the audited financial statements (e.g., MD&A revenue trend statements that contradict audited revenue figures) or a material misstatement of fact (incorrect data not related to the financial statements). If such matters are identified, the auditor takes appropriate action — discussing with management and, if unresolved, considering the implications for the audit report.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: other information in documents containing audited financial statements
questions.text: The auditor reads the MD&A section of a public company's annual report and notes that management describes gross profit margin as having 'increased by 3.2%' during the year. The audited financial statements show that gross profit margin actually decreased by 1.8% from the prior year. This is MOST appropriately characterized as

answers.text: An immaterial rounding difference that requires no action under AU-C 720

A material inconsistency between other information and the audited financial statements — the auditor should discuss the discrepancy with management and determine whether the MD&A or the financial statements require revision
A material misstatement of fact — the MD&A contains factual information unrelated to the financial statements
An emphasis-of-matter situation requiring the auditor to add a paragraph to the audit report

explanations.a: A 5-percentage-point discrepancy between what MD&A states (3.2% increase) and what the audited statements show (1.8% decrease) is not a rounding difference — it is a significant, directionally opposite discrepancy. Even if the dollar amount appeared small, the directional error (increase vs. decrease) would mislead users about the entity's performance trend.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 720 defines a material inconsistency as an inconsistency between other information and the audited financial statements that indicates the financial statements or other information may need to be restated. When MD&A states that gross profit margin increased while the audited statements show it decreased, the auditor has identified a material inconsistency. The auditor should: discuss the inconsistency with management; determine whether it is the MD&A or the financial statements that are correct; and request management to revise the inconsistent information. If management refuses, the auditor considers whether to include an other-matter paragraph in the report.
explanations.c: A material misstatement of fact involves other information that contains factually incorrect statements not directly related to the financial statements — for example, incorrect biographical information about management. This discrepancy is a material inconsistency (conflict between other information and the audited statements), not a misstatement of fact unrelated to the financial statements.
explanations.d: An emphasis-of-matter paragraph draws attention to matters already properly disclosed in the financial statements. A material inconsistency in the MD&A is not resolved by adding a paragraph to the financial statement report — it requires revision of the inconsistent information or appropriate communication if unresolved.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: other information in documents containing audited financial statements
questions.text: An auditor reads an annual report's narrative section and notices that it states the entity 'employs over 5,000 people worldwide.' The auditor's knowledge from the audit suggests the entity has approximately 2,800 employees based on payroll records reviewed. This is MOST appropriately characterized as

answers.text: An immaterial misstatement since employee counts are not financial data and do not affect the financial statements
A material inconsistency between the other information and the audited financial statements — requiring the same response as a discrepancy in financial data

A material misstatement of fact in the other information — the statement about employee count appears factually incorrect and inconsistent with information the auditor obtained during the audit, warranting discussion with management
Not an auditor concern since employee count is a management-controlled disclosure that the auditor has no obligation to evaluate

explanations.a: Incorrect non-financial data can be material regardless of its direct impact on financial statement numbers. Users of annual reports rely on narrative information — including employee counts — to assess the scale of the entity. A 75% overstatement of employee count could significantly affect users' assessments of the entity's size and capabilities.
explanations.b: A material inconsistency under AU-C 720 refers to a conflict between other information and the audited financial statements. Employee count is not a financial statement figure — so this is not an inconsistency with the financial statements. Instead, it falls into the category of a material misstatement of fact.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 720 requires the auditor to consider whether other information contains a material misstatement of fact — factually incorrect information not directly related to the audited financial statements. An employee count that appears to be nearly double the actual headcount based on payroll records reviewed during the audit is a potential material misstatement of fact. The auditor should discuss the discrepancy with management to understand whether the count includes contractors, part-time workers, or other personnel not captured in payroll — and if management cannot support the stated count, the auditor should request a correction.
explanations.d: AU-C 720 specifically requires the auditor to consider whether other information contains material misstatements of fact. While the auditor does not audit the other information, they do have an obligation to consider information that appears factually incorrect based on knowledge obtained during the audit.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A review of interim financial information (such as quarterly financial statements filed on Form 10-Q by an SEC registrant) provides which level of assurance?

answers.text: Reasonable assurance — equivalent to the annual audit opinion
Absolute assurance — the quarterly statements are certified as accurate
Limited assurance — expressed in a negative-form conclusion stating that nothing came to the auditor's attention indicating material modifications are needed
No assurance — the review is informational only and makes no conclusion about the quarterly statements

explanations.a: A review of interim financial information provides limited assurance — not the reasonable assurance of an annual financial statement audit. The scope of review procedures (primarily inquiries and analytical procedures) is much narrower than an audit.
explanations.b: Absolute assurance is not provided by any professional engagement. Interim reviews, with their limited scope, provide even less assurance than audits.
explanations.c: Both PCAOB AS 4105 (for issuers) and AU-C 930 (for nonissuers) establish that a review of interim financial information results in limited assurance expressed in negative form: 'Based on our review, we are not aware of any material modifications that should be made to the accompanying interim financial information for it to be in accordance with [GAAP].' This negative framing reflects that the procedures did not detect evidence of material misstatement — not that no misstatements exist.
explanations.d: A review does provide assurance — specifically limited assurance through a practitioner's negative-form conclusion. It is not informational only — it is an assurance engagement with a defined output.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: Who typically performs the review of interim financial information for an SEC registrant?

answers.text: The internal audit department — since they have continuous access to the entity's financial records throughout the year
A different audit firm than the annual auditor — to provide independence of the quarterly review
Management itself, with the results disclosed in the 10-Q filing
The independent registered public accounting firm that audits the entity's annual financial statements — providing continuity and contextual knowledge critical for effective interim review

explanations.a: Internal audit performs work for management and does not provide independent assurance. Interim reviews requiring a practitioner's conclusion must be performed by an independent external auditor — not by internal audit.
explanations.b: Using a different audit firm for quarterly reviews than for annual audits would sacrifice the knowledge continuity that makes interim reviews effective. The quarterly reviewer needs detailed knowledge of the entity, its accounting policies, and its risk areas — knowledge best held by the annual auditor.
explanations.c: Management prepares the quarterly financial statements but does not perform the review. SEC requirements for reviews of quarterly financial information (Securities Exchange Act Rule 10-01) require involvement of an independent public accounting firm.
explanations.d: PCAOB AS 4105 and SEC rules contemplate that the principal auditor — the firm that audits the annual financial statements — also performs the review of interim financial information. This arrangement provides: the reviewer's existing knowledge of the entity's business, accounting policies, and risk areas; continuity between quarterly and annual procedures; and efficiency in identifying issues that may carry through to the annual audit.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: The primary procedures performed during a review of interim financial information consist of

answers.text: Inquiries of management about the entity's accounting policies, significant transactions, and whether the interim information is prepared in accordance with GAAP, combined with analytical procedures to identify unusual relationships or amounts requiring further inquiry
Tests of controls and detailed substantive testing of all significant account balances — the same procedures as an annual audit applied to a shorter period
Physical observation of inventory, external confirmations of receivables, and recalculations of selected financial statement totals
A comparison of quarterly results to the most recently completed annual audit — if the quarterly amounts appear consistent with the annual period, limited assurance is established

explanations.a: PCAOB AS 4105 and AU-C 930 specify that a review of interim financial information consists primarily of: (1) inquiries of management knowledgeable about the entity's financial reporting — covering accounting policies, significant new transactions, unusual items, significant estimates, and changes from the prior year; and (2) analytical procedures — comparing current-period interim information to prior periods, expected patterns, and non-financial data. These procedures form the basis for the limited assurance conclusion.
explanations.b: Tests of controls and detailed substantive testing are audit-level procedures. Applying them to a shorter period does not make the engagement a review — it would make it a quarterly audit. The scope of interim reviews is intentionally limited to inquiries and analytics.
explanations.c: Physical inventory observation, accounts receivable confirmations, and financial statement recalculations are substantive audit procedures. These are not the defining procedures of an interim review.
explanations.d: Simply comparing quarterly amounts to the annual audit is an overly simplistic analytical comparison that does not constitute the required review procedures. Quarterly interim reviews require specific current-period inquiries and analytical procedures — not just reference to prior annual audit conclusions.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: During an interim review of an SEC issuer's Q3 financial statements, the auditor's analytical procedures identify that revenue increased 40% quarter-over-quarter with no corresponding increase in accounts receivable — suggesting revenue may have been recognized without underlying transactions. Management's explanation is that the increase was due to a large one-time sale that was collected immediately at the time of delivery. How should the auditor respond?

answers.text: Accept management's explanation since it is plausible and the procedures performed were sufficient for a limited-assurance engagement
Issue a modified interim review conclusion immediately based on the analytical finding

Expand the inquiry and make additional inquiries specifically about this transaction — requesting documentation of the large sale, the delivery evidence, and the immediate cash collection to evaluate whether management's explanation is corroborated
Conclude that the analytical pattern proves fraudulent revenue recognition and report the finding to the SEC

explanations.a: While management's explanation is plausible (large, immediately-collected sales do occur), plausibility alone is not sufficient when the analytical result indicates a significant unusual pattern. The combination of a 40% revenue increase with no receivable growth is a red flag that warrants further inquiry — especially given the revenue fraud risk environment.
explanations.b: Immediately issuing a modified conclusion based solely on an analytical finding — before any follow-up — would be premature. The appropriate first step is additional inquiry, not immediate report modification.
explanations.c: PCAOB AS 4105 and AU-C 930 require the auditor to make additional inquiries when analytical procedures produce unexpected results. For a significant revenue anomaly, the auditor should: inquire specifically about the large one-time sale; request supporting documentation (customer purchase order, shipping documents, evidence of delivery, cash receipt records); evaluate whether the cash collection timing and amount is consistent with the explanation; and consider whether the transaction was recorded in accordance with applicable revenue recognition guidance. Additional inquiry within the review framework is the appropriate response before drawing conclusions.
explanations.d: An analytical procedure finding indicates a risk that warrants investigation — it is not proof of fraud. The auditor must investigate through additional inquiries and evaluation before drawing fraud conclusions. Additionally, the auditor does not report potential fraud directly to the SEC from within an interim review — the response process begins with management inquiry and escalation to TCWG if needed.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: supplementary information in relation to financial statements as a whole
questions.text: When the auditor reports on supplementary information under AU-C Section 725, the auditor's opinion on the supplementary information is expressed as

answers.text: A positive opinion stating the supplementary information is fairly presented in conformity with the applicable financial reporting framework — independent of the financial statements
A negative conclusion stating that nothing came to the auditor's attention indicating the supplementary information is misstated
No assurance — the auditor only reads supplementary information without providing any form of conclusion

An opinion on whether the supplementary information is fairly stated in all material respects in relation to the financial statements as a whole — not whether it independently conforms to the full applicable framework

explanations.a: The opinion on supplementary information under AU-C 725 is 'in relation to the financial statements as a whole' — not an independent opinion on conformity with the full applicable framework. This is a meaningful distinction: the supplementary information is evaluated as a complement to the financial statements, not as a standalone set of statements.
explanations.b: A negative conclusion is the output of review-level assurance engagements, not the opinion on supplementary information. AU-C 725 results in a positive-form opinion ('in our opinion, the supplementary information is fairly stated in all material respects in relation to the financial statements as a whole').
explanations.c: Under AU-C 725, the auditor actively reports on supplementary information — providing assurance through a specific opinion. This differs from AU-C 720 (other information), where the auditor only reads and considers without providing an opinion.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 725 establishes that when auditors report on supplementary information, they express an opinion on whether it is 'fairly stated, in all material respects, in relation to the financial statements as a whole.' The 'in relation to' standard means the supplementary information is evaluated for consistency with and derivation from the audited financial statements — not for independent conformity with all elements of the applicable reporting framework.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: supplementary information in relation to financial statements as a whole
questions.text: When reporting on supplementary information under AU-C Section 725, the auditor performs certain procedures. Which of the following procedures is MOST characteristic of this reporting?

answers.text: Performing a separate full audit of the supplementary information with the same scope as the financial statement audit

Inquiring of management about the purpose and preparation of the supplementary information, comparing and reconciling it to the underlying accounting records and audited financial statements, and performing additional procedures as appropriate
Reading the supplementary information and considering whether it appears inconsistent with the financial statements — without performing any reconciliation or substantive procedures
Relying entirely on management's written representations that the supplementary information is fairly presented

explanations.a: A full separate audit of supplementary information is not required under AU-C 725 — and would be disproportionate given that the opinion is expressed 'in relation to the financial statements' rather than as a standalone audit. The procedures are more focused than a full audit.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 725 requires the auditor to perform specific procedures for supplementary information including: (1) inquiring of management about the purpose of the supplementary information and the method of its preparation; (2) comparing and reconciling the supplementary information to the underlying accounting records and to the audited financial statements to ensure consistency; (3) agreeing or reconciling amounts to supporting schedules; and (4) evaluating whether the supplementary information is fairly stated in relation to the financial statements as a whole. These procedures provide the basis for the 'in relation to' opinion.
explanations.c: Reading and considering without further procedures describes the AU-C 720 other information standard. AU-C 725 supplementary information requires more active engagement — reconciliation and substantive comparison procedures that go beyond merely reading.
explanations.d: Management representations are supplementary to other evidence — they do not substitute for the procedures required by AU-C 725. The reconciliation and comparison procedures are essential to the audit basis for the opinion.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: supplementary information in relation to financial statements as a whole
questions.text: An auditor is reporting on supplementary schedule that presents segment revenue by geographic region — supplementary to the audited consolidated financial statements. The total segment revenues on the supplementary schedule differ from consolidated revenues in the audited statements by an amount that cannot be reconciled. How should the auditor respond?

answers.text: Issue the supplementary information opinion without modification since reconciling differences are expected in segment reporting
Issue the financial statement opinion but exclude any opinion on the supplementary information without explanation

Investigate the unreconcilable difference, determine whether it represents a material misstatement in the supplementary information, and if management refuses to correct a material difference, consider declining to report on the supplementary information or modifying the opinion on it
Automatically issue an adverse opinion on the supplementary information since any unreconciled difference constitutes a material departure

explanations.a: An unreconcilable difference between supplementary information and the audited financial statements is a significant issue — it potentially indicates that the supplementary information is not consistent with or derivable from the financial statements. This cannot be dismissed as an expected reconciling difference.
explanations.b: Simply excluding the supplementary opinion without explanation would not adequately communicate to users that the supplementary information could not be reconciled to the financial statements. If the auditor declines to report on the supplementary information, this should be disclosed.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 725 requires the auditor to reconcile the supplementary information to the audited financial statements as part of the reporting procedures. An unreconcilable difference requires investigation to determine its source. If the difference is a material misstatement in the supplementary information and management refuses to correct it, the auditor should: either modify the opinion on the supplementary information to note the material departure; or withdraw from reporting on the supplementary information if circumstances require. The response is proportional to the severity of the unresolved difference.
explanations.d: An adverse opinion on supplementary information requires a conclusion that the information is materially misstated — the unreconcilable difference first requires investigation before the auditor can reach this conclusion. An automatic adverse opinion without investigation would be premature.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: supplementary information in relation to financial statements as a whole
questions.text: An entity's pension plan financial statements include a required supplementary information (RSI) schedule showing the funded status trend over 10 years. The Government Accounting Standards Board (GASB) requires this RSI for governmental plan audits. The auditor is auditing the pension plan's financial statements. Regarding the RSI, the auditor's obligation is

answers.text: To apply the same audit procedures to the RSI as to the basic financial statements and express an opinion on the RSI

To read the RSI to determine whether it is consistent with the financial statements, identify whether required information appears to be missing, and consider whether there are apparent material misstatements — then communicate findings to management; the auditor does not express an opinion on RSI
To decline to issue an audit report if RSI is not included in the reporting document
To verify every line in the RSI by performing substantive procedures on each year's data presented in the 10-year trend

explanations.a: RSI is not audited — the auditor's obligation is limited and does not include expressing an opinion on RSI. Performing full audit procedures on RSI would overstate the auditor's responsibility and imply an opinion is being expressed.
explanations.b: For required supplementary information, the auditor's obligation (under AU-C 730) is to: (1) inquire of management about the methods of preparing the RSI; (2) compare the RSI for consistency with the financial statements; (3) apply analytical procedures to the RSI; (4) read the RSI and consider whether any required information appears missing; and (5) determine whether any apparent material misstatements exist. The auditor does NOT express an opinion on RSI — they report on whether the RSI is measured and presented within prescribed guidelines based on these limited procedures. RSI sits between 'other information' (no procedures) and supplementary information under AU-C 725 (opinion expressed).
explanations.c: RSI may sometimes be omitted or presented with omissions or departures from GASB requirements — the auditor addresses such issues in the auditor's report but does not decline to issue a report solely on this basis. The procedures and any findings related to RSI are addressed in the audit report.
explanations.d: Performing substantive procedures on every line of a 10-year RSI schedule would be audit-level testing that exceeds the required scope. The auditor's RSI obligations under AU-C 730 are limited — inquiry, analytical procedures, comparison to financial statements, and consideration of apparent misstatements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: additional reporting under GAO Government Auditing Standards
questions.text: When a financial audit is conducted under Government Auditing Standards (Yellow Book), the auditor must issue additional reports beyond the standard financial statement opinion. These additional required reports are

answers.text: A report on internal control over financial reporting AND a report on compliance with laws, regulations, and provisions of contracts and grant agreements — both based on the audit procedures performed
A performance audit report evaluating whether the entity's programs achieved their intended outcomes
A fraud investigation report identifying all instances of fraud detected during the audit
A management effectiveness report and a report on the entity's strategic plan

explanations.a: Government Auditing Standards (2018 GAGAS, paragraph 6.02) require auditors performing financial audits to issue two reports in addition to the financial statement audit opinion: (1) a report on internal control over financial reporting — describing significant deficiencies, material weaknesses, and other control matters identified; and (2) a report on compliance with laws, regulations, and provisions of contracts and grant agreements — communicating noncompliance identified during the audit. These additional reports fulfill GAGAS's public accountability objectives beyond what is required by GAAS alone.
explanations.b: Performance audit reports are issued in GAGAS performance audit engagements — a completely separate type of engagement from financial audits. Performance audits evaluate program economy, efficiency, and effectiveness. They are not additional reports required in a financial audit.
explanations.c: A fraud investigation report is not a standard required report in a GAGAS financial audit. The GAGAS financial audit does require reporting of identified fraud, but this is communicated within the compliance report or through separate communications to appropriate officials — not through a standalone fraud investigation report.
explanations.d: Management effectiveness reports and strategic plan reports are not GAGAS financial audit requirements. These would be separate performance audit or consulting engagements, not additional reports within the financial audit framework.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: additional reporting under GAO Government Auditing Standards
questions.text: The GAGAS report on internal control differs from an ICFR opinion in an integrated audit (PCAOB AS 2201) primarily in that

answers.text: The GAGAS IC report covers only controls related to federal compliance; the PCAOB ICFR opinion covers financial reporting controls

The GAGAS IC report describes identified deficiencies and other control matters identified during the financial audit but does not express an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control as a whole — while the PCAOB ICFR opinion directly opines on whether ICFR is effective
The GAGAS IC report is issued annually; the PCAOB ICFR opinion is issued only when material weaknesses are found
The GAGAS IC report is required only for entities receiving more than $10 million in federal funding

explanations.a: The GAGAS IC report covers internal control over financial reporting broadly — not only compliance-related controls. While GAGAS has separate compliance considerations, the IC report addresses the overall control environment and financial reporting controls identified during the audit.
explanations.b: This accurately distinguishes the two reports. The GAGAS report on internal control communicates findings about significant deficiencies, material weaknesses, and other matters identified during the financial audit — it is a findings-based communication report. It does not express an opinion on whether ICFR is effective overall. In contrast, the PCAOB AS 2201 ICFR opinion directly states whether 'management's assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting is fairly stated' and whether ICFR 'is effective as of [date]' — a positive opinion (or adverse if a material weakness exists). This is a substantive difference in the nature of the conclusion.
explanations.c: Both the GAGAS IC report and the PCAOB ICFR opinion are issued annually (for fiscal periods covered by the respective audits). The PCAOB ICFR opinion is not conditional on finding material weaknesses — it is required in all integrated audits.
explanations.d: The GAGAS IC report requirement applies based on whether the engagement is performed under GAGAS — not on a specific federal funding threshold. Any entity for which a GAGAS audit is required must receive the additional reports.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: additional reporting under GAO Government Auditing Standards
questions.text: An auditor performing a GAGAS financial audit identifies a significant deficiency in internal control related to the reconciliation of grant expenditures. The GAGAS report on internal control should

answers.text: Omit the significant deficiency since it is below the material weakness threshold and GAGAS only requires reporting of material weaknesses
Include the significant deficiency as a reportable finding — GAGAS requires reporting of significant deficiencies AND material weaknesses in the internal control report
Report the significant deficiency only if it also resulted in a material misstatement in the financial statements
Include the finding but qualify it as 'low risk' since significant deficiencies do not represent a high-level concern

explanations.a: GAGAS requirements go beyond GAAS in what must be reported in the internal control report. Under GAGAS, both significant deficiencies AND material weaknesses must be communicated in the internal control report — not only material weaknesses. This is more expansive than the GAAS requirement (which also requires both to be communicated in writing under AU-C 265, but GAGAS makes this a specific report-inclusion requirement).
explanations.b: The 2018 Yellow Book (paragraph 6.28) requires the auditor's report on internal control to include findings about significant deficiencies and material weaknesses identified during the audit, presented in the format required by GAGAS (condition, criteria, cause, effect). A significant deficiency in grant expenditure reconciliation is a reportable finding in the GAGAS internal control report — not something that can be omitted because it falls below the material weakness threshold.
explanations.c: Financial statement impact is relevant to severity classification, but a significant deficiency is reportable in the GAGAS IC report regardless of whether it actually resulted in a material misstatement in the current period. The risk of future misstatement and the public accountability purpose of GAGAS reporting justify disclosure even without a current-period financial statement impact.
explanations.d: GAGAS does not categorize findings as 'low risk' or use such labels to qualify findings. Significant deficiencies are reported based on their nature and potential impact — not labeled with risk assessments that would minimize their significance in the public report.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.keyword: additional reporting under GAO Government Auditing Standards
questions.text: Under Government Auditing Standards, when auditors identify fraud or suspected illegal acts during a GAGAS financial audit, how must they communicate this information?

answers.text: Only in the management letter — fraud and illegal acts are confidential and cannot be reported in public audit documents

To management and those charged with governance of the entity — and potentially to regulatory or law enforcement authorities if the matter involves a government program and TCWG appears unwilling to take appropriate action
Directly to law enforcement without informing management, since informing management could obstruct the investigation
Only to the entity's external legal counsel, who then determines how to proceed

explanations.a: GAGAS fraud and illegal act communication is not limited to a confidential management letter. Government auditing's public accountability mission requires broader communication — and in some cases, the matters must be included in the public audit reports.
explanations.b: GAGAS (paragraph 6.33-6.40) requires auditors who identify fraud or illegal acts to: (1) communicate to management and those charged with governance — to enable them to take remedial action; (2) consider whether the matter should be reported to external parties such as regulatory oversight agencies (e.g., state legislature, federal agency) — particularly when the entity's management or TCWG appears implicated or unwilling to respond; and (3) in some cases, include the matter in the public audit reports. The communication hierarchy addresses multiple parties to fulfill GAGAS's accountability requirements.
explanations.c: Bypassing management entirely and going directly to law enforcement is not the GAGAS approach. Auditors first communicate to management and TCWG, then escalate if management fails to respond appropriately. Additionally, sudden law enforcement notification could obstruct proper remediation through official channels.
explanations.d: Communicating only to external legal counsel without management or TCWG notification is not the GAGAS requirement. While legal counsel may be consulted about the matter, the communication obligations run to management, TCWG, and potentially regulatory authorities — not exclusively to legal counsel.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A special-purpose financial reporting framework (SPF) is BEST described as

answers.text: A customized version of GAAP developed by individual companies for internal management reporting purposes
A financial reporting framework mandated by the SEC for smaller reporting companies
A financial reporting framework other than GAAP — including cash basis, tax basis, regulatory basis (e.g., statutory accounting for insurance), and contractual basis frameworks
International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) applied to entities that operate internationally

explanations.a: Internal management reporting frameworks are not what AU-C 800 addresses. Special-purpose frameworks under AU-C 800 are used for external reporting to specific audiences — not internal reporting. Management accounts prepared only for internal use may follow any internal framework without triggering AU-C 800 considerations.
explanations.b: The SEC does not mandate an SPF for smaller reporting companies — SEC registrants generally use US GAAP (or IFRS for foreign private issuers). An SPF is an alternative to GAAP, not a variation mandated by the SEC for specific registrant categories.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 800 defines a special-purpose framework as a financial reporting basis other than GAAP. Examples include: (1) cash basis — recognizing transactions when cash is received or paid; (2) tax basis — using income tax principles as the reporting basis; (3) regulatory basis — frameworks prescribed by regulatory bodies (such as statutory accounting principles for insurance companies prescribed by state insurance regulators); and (4) contractual basis — frameworks required by the terms of an agreement (such as specific accounting for a partnership or joint venture agreement). These frameworks may produce financial statements that materially differ from GAAP.
explanations.d: IFRS is a comprehensive, generally accepted financial reporting framework in its own right — not a special-purpose framework. The AICPA and PCAOB recognize both US GAAP and IFRS as acceptable frameworks for financial statement audits. SPFs are frameworks distinct from both GAAP and IFRS.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: When an auditor reports on financial statements prepared on a tax basis of accounting (a special-purpose framework), the auditor's report must include

answers.text: An emphasis-of-matter paragraph identifying the tax basis of accounting, explaining that the financial statements are prepared in accordance with tax principles rather than GAAP, and noting that the basis may differ from GAAP in material respects
A qualified opinion since tax-basis financial statements always depart from GAAP in at least some material respects
A disclaimer of opinion because tax-basis financial statements cannot be fairly presented without GAAP application
No special disclosures — the standard audit report format is unchanged for special-purpose framework audits

explanations.a: AU-C Section 800 requires that when auditing financial statements prepared using a special-purpose framework, the auditor's report must include: (1) an emphasis-of-matter paragraph identifying the basis of accounting used (tax basis in this case); (2) a reference to the note disclosing the basis; and (3) for cash basis and tax basis frameworks, a statement that the basis differs from GAAP. This emphasis paragraph alerts users to understand that the statements follow a different framework and cannot be directly compared to GAAP-based financial statements. The paragraph does not modify the audit opinion — the auditor still expresses an unmodified opinion if the financial statements are fairly presented in accordance with the tax basis.
explanations.b: A qualified opinion is issued when a material misstatement exists or there is a scope limitation — not simply because financial statements are prepared on a tax basis. If the tax-basis statements are fairly presented in accordance with tax principles, an unmodified opinion is appropriate with the SPF emphasis paragraph.
explanations.c: A disclaimer of opinion arises from pervasive scope limitations — not from the use of a special-purpose framework. Financial statements prepared on a tax basis can be fairly presented and receive an unmodified opinion.
explanations.d: The standard audit report format requires modification for SPF engagements. AU-C 800 specifically prescribes additional elements — including the emphasis-of-matter paragraph identifying the basis — that differ from the standard GAAS financial statement audit report.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: A partnership uses a contractual basis of accounting as required by its partnership agreement — recognizing revenues on a modified cash basis and treating certain capital expenditures differently than GAAP. The auditor is evaluating whether this contractual framework is a suitable reporting basis for the audit. What factor is MOST important in this evaluation?

answers.text: Whether the contractual framework matches GAAP as closely as possible — the fewer deviations from GAAP, the more suitable the framework
Whether the contractual framework has been approved by the FASB as an acceptable alternative to GAAP
Whether the contractual framework produces financial statements that could mislead users who are unfamiliar with it — if so, the framework is not suitable regardless of the contractual requirement

Whether the framework is intended for use by specified users who are knowledgeable about the basis and its limitations, and whether the financial statements include adequate disclosures to allow users to understand the basis and its significant differences from GAAP

explanations.a: The suitability of a special-purpose framework is not determined by its proximity to GAAP. SPFs are legitimate alternatives with their own coherent logic — contractual basis frameworks are designed to serve the specific needs of the contracting parties, not to approximate GAAP.
explanations.b: The FASB does not approve or certify special-purpose frameworks. Contractual basis frameworks are established by the terms of agreements — they derive their authority from the contractual arrangement, not from accounting standard-setter approval.
explanations.c: While the potential for user misunderstanding is relevant, the solution for contractual-basis frameworks is typically adequate disclosure — not abandoning the framework. AU-C 800 recognizes that SPF financial statements are often used by specified, knowledgeable parties who understand the basis; the presence of disclosure requirements addresses the user understanding concern.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 800 evaluates the suitability of special-purpose frameworks based on: (1) whether the framework is intended for use by specified parties who understand the basis; (2) whether adequate disclosures will enable users to understand the basis of accounting and how it differs from GAAP; and (3) whether the framework as applied would produce financial statements that are reliable and informative for the intended users. Contractual-basis frameworks are generally suitable when the contracting parties understand the framework and the financial statements are adequately disclosed — this is the primary evaluative standard.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Forming Conclusions and Reporting
questions.text: An insurance company prepares financial statements using Statutory Accounting Principles (SAP) — a regulatory basis SPF mandated by state insurance regulators. The SAP statements differ from GAAP in several material ways: SAP requires immediate expensing of certain acquisition costs that GAAP would capitalize, uses different reserving methodologies, and prohibits certain asset types recognized under GAAP. The auditor is evaluating the appropriate report to issue. Which conclusion is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: Issue an adverse opinion because SAP financial statements always differ materially from GAAP and therefore cannot be 'fairly presented'

Issue an unmodified opinion on the SAP financial statements — with an emphasis-of-matter paragraph identifying the regulatory basis (SAP), referring to the relevant note disclosures, and potentially restricting use of the report to specified regulatory users — since fair presentation is evaluated against the SAP framework, not GAAP
Issue a qualified opinion for each SAP departure from GAAP since each difference is a departure from accepted accounting principles
Decline to issue any opinion on SAP financial statements since only GAAP-based statements can be the subject of an audit opinion

explanations.a: 'Fair presentation' in the context of SAP financial statements is evaluated against the SAP framework — not GAAP. SAP is a coherent, complete regulatory framework developed specifically for insurance companies to assess solvency and protect policyholders. Financial statements that are fairly presented in accordance with SAP are not materially misstated simply because they differ from GAAP — they differ because the frameworks have different objectives. An adverse opinion would be wholly inappropriate for properly prepared SAP statements.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 800 provides that when auditing regulatory-basis financial statements (such as SAP), the auditor expresses an opinion on whether the statements are 'presented fairly in all material respects in accordance with the regulatory framework' — not in accordance with GAAP. An unmodified opinion is appropriate if the SAP statements are fairly presented within the SAP framework. The report must include: (1) an emphasis-of-matter paragraph identifying the regulatory basis; (2) a statement noting the basis may differ from GAAP in material respects; (3) reference to the note disclosing the basis; and (4) potentially a restriction on use if the regulatory framework is only for specified users (state insurance regulators and specified parties), since regulatory-basis statements may not be appropriate for general public distribution.
explanations.c: The SAP differences from GAAP are not 'departures' from accepted principles — SAP is itself an accepted regulatory framework. Issuing a qualified opinion for each SAP feature that differs from GAAP would mischaracterize the engagement; the auditor is evaluating against SAP, not GAAP.
explanations.d: CPAs regularly audit and opine on special-purpose framework financial statements including SAP, OCBOA (Other Comprehensive Bases of Accounting), and other regulatory frameworks. AU-C 800 specifically provides for such audits and opinions.
